entries.description: Light bounced into or shot through an umbrella, spilling widely and lighting the whole room along with the subject. Round catchlights, sometimes with visible ribs. Less controlled than [softbox_lighting](#softbox_lighting).

entries.name: background_light
entries.description: A lamp aimed at the backdrop rather than the subject, lifting it off black or laying a pool or gradient behind the head. Tag it when the backdrop is visibly lit on its own. For a coloured wash use [gelled_light](#gelled_light) as well.

entries.name: continuous_lighting
entries.description: Steady lamps or panels rather than [flash](#flash), so the exposure records whatever movement happened. Common for video-adjacent stills and for tabletop work where you want to see the lighting as you set it.

entries.name: gelled_light
entries.description: Coloured gel over a studio source, washing the backdrop or the subject in one strong hue, often two contrasting colours from either side. Tag the deliberate studio colour, not a scene that simply happens to have coloured lamps in it.

entries.name: green_screen
entries.description: An evenly lit saturated green or blue backdrop meant to be replaced later, usually with green spill on the subject's edges. Tag the unreplaced original; a finished composite belongs with the editing tags.

entries.name: gridded_light
entries.description: A honeycomb grid on the source narrowing the beam so it falls only where it is aimed, with visible falloff at the edge of the pool. Used to keep light off the backdrop or to light one feature. A tighter cone still is a [snoot](#snoot).

entries.name: lighting_ratio
entries.description: Tag pictures where the balance between key and fill is the point — a flat two-to-one for catalogue work, a steep eight-to-one for drama. Useful when the setup is otherwise plain but the contrast choice is deliberate.

entries.name: negative_fill
entries.description: Black panels or flags placed near the subject to take light away and deepen the shadow side. Look for shadows darker than the room would allow and a crisp falloff along the far cheek. The opposite move is [reflector_fill](#reflector_fill).

entries.name: painted_backdrop
entries.description: A hand-painted or mottled canvas or muslin behind the subject, its brush texture and uneven tone plainly visible. Typical of classic and school portraiture. A flat untextured roll is a [seamless_backdrop](#seamless_backdrop) instead.

entries.name: strip_light
entries.description: A long narrow [softbox](#softbox) used to run a soft band down the side of a body, a bottle or a car. Leaves a tall thin [catchlight](#catchlight) and a controlled highlight edge. Two of them either side is the classic product setup.

entries.name: cyclorama
entries.description: A built curved wall-to-floor cove, large enough to stand or drive into, giving a horizonless white space. Bigger and more permanent than a [seamless_backdrop](#seamless_backdrop), and the corners are plastered rather than rolled.

entries.name: light_tent
entries.description: A small translucent box or cube with the object inside and lights outside, giving wraparound shadowless illumination for products and small goods. Look for near-invisible shadows and a soft even sweep under the object.

entries.name: correct_exposure
entries.description: The brightness sits where it was meant to: highlights hold detail, shadows are not blocked up, skin and midtones read naturally. Use it as the neutral answer when neither [overexposed](#overexposed) nor [underexposed](#underexposed) applies. It says nothing about contrast, so pair it with [high_contrast](#high_contrast) or [low_contrast](#low_contrast) when that matters.

entries.name: blown_highlights
entries.description: The brightest areas have clipped to pure white with no texture left in them. Common in a bright sky, a lamp, or sunlit skin. The rest of the frame can still be [correct_exposure](#correct_exposure), which is why this is its own tag rather than a flavour of [overexposed](#overexposed).

entries.name: high_contrast
entries.description: A wide gap between the light and dark parts of the frame, with little sitting in between. Edges look punchy and shadows fall away fast. Say what the tone does, not what caused it; a merely bright picture is not this.

entries.name: low_contrast
entries.description: The tones sit close together, with no real black and no real white in the frame. Typical of an overcast day, a hazy view or a soft scan. If it also looks faded and lifted rather than simply gentle, reach for [washed_out](#washed_out).

entries.name: overexposed
entries.description: Too much light reached the sensor or film, so the whole picture sits too bright and pale. Judge it on the overall level, not on a single bright patch. If only the brightest areas have gone to paper white, use [blown_highlights](#blown_highlights) instead.

entries.name: silhouette
entries.description: The subject is a black shape against a much brighter background, with its own detail given up entirely. Exposure was set for the background. If some detail survives in the shape, use [partial_silhouette](#partial_silhouette).

entries.name: underexposed
entries.description: Too little light reached the sensor or film, so the picture is darker than intended and the shadows go muddy. Deliberate darkness for effect is [low_key](#low_key), not this. If only the darkest areas have lost all detail, use [crushed_blacks](#crushed_blacks).

entries.name: auto_exposure
entries.description: The camera chose the exposure, as most phone and point-and-shoot pictures are made. Worth recording when the automatic choice explains a blown sky or a bright subject. The counterpart is [manual_exposure](#manual_exposure).

entries.name: blown_sky
entries.description: The sky has clipped to featureless white while the ground is correctly exposed, the usual result of metering for the land. A naturally bright but still detailed grey sky is not this.

entries.name: crushed_blacks
entries.description: The darkest areas have gone to solid black with nothing readable inside them. Sometimes a deliberate look, sometimes the price of exposing for the highlights. Deep but still detailed shadows are [deep_blacks](#deep_blacks), and a whole picture that is simply too dark is [underexposed](#underexposed).

entries.name: deep_blacks
entries.description: Rich, dense shadows that still hold some texture, giving the frame weight and a solid bottom end. The opposite of [lifted_blacks](#lifted_blacks). If nothing at all can be read in the dark areas, that is [crushed_blacks](#crushed_blacks).

entries.name: exposed_for_the_highlights
entries.description: The bright end was protected and the shadows were allowed to fall where they may, so the sky or the lamp keeps its texture while the dark areas go heavy. Often ends up beside [crushed_blacks](#crushed_blacks) or [silhouette](#silhouette).

entries.name: exposure_compensation
entries.description: The meter's reading was deliberately overridden by a stop or so, brightening a snow scene or holding a stage back. Use it when the file or the description says so, not as a guess about intent.

entries.name: flat_tones
entries.description: The tonal range is compressed into a narrow band, so the picture reads as dull and lifeless with nothing anchoring either end. Often how a raw file or a log-style capture looks before grading. It is a stronger claim than [low_contrast](#low_contrast), which can still be pleasant.

entries.name: high_dynamic_range
entries.description: The picture holds detail across a range no single frame normally captures, from open shadows to an unclipped sky. Made by combining exposures or by heavy shadow and highlight work. For the crunchy, over-processed version of the look, add [tone_mapped](#tone_mapped).

entries.name: lifted_blacks
entries.description: The darkest tone in the picture is a soft grey rather than black, giving the matte, filmic feel of a faded print. Usually a deliberate curve. The whole picture being pale and weak is [washed_out](#washed_out); this is about the shadow end alone.

entries.name: manual_exposure
entries.description: Shutter and aperture were set by hand and held there, so the exposure stays the same from frame to frame regardless of what the meter says. Common in studio and stage work.

entries.name: washed_out
entries.description: Faded and milky, as if a grey veil sits over everything: blacks are grey, colours are weak, nothing bites. Caused by [haze](#haze), flare, a tired print or a heavy fade look. Use [lifted_blacks](#lifted_blacks) when the shadows alone are raised and the rest holds up.

entries.name: backlight_compensation
entries.description: Exposure was pushed up so a subject against a bright window or sky keeps its face, accepting that the background blows out. The opposite decision gives a [silhouette](#silhouette).

entries.name: blown_window
entries.description: An interior shot where the windows have gone solid white so the room can be seen. Very common in room and interview pictures. Balancing the two instead usually means [high_dynamic_range](#high_dynamic_range) or a [flash](#flash).

entries.name: dodged_and_burned
entries.description: Parts of the frame were lightened or darkened by hand, so brightness varies in a way the light in the room does not explain — a lifted face, a darkened corner. Look for soft-edged patches that do not follow the shadows.

entries.name: exposed_for_the_shadows
entries.description: Exposure was set so the dark parts stay open and readable, accepting that the brightest areas clip. The usual companion of [blown_highlights](#blown_highlights) in a [backlit](#backlit) or window-lit scene.

entries.name: exposure_blending
entries.description: Two or more differently exposed frames merged into one, taking sky from the dark frame and shadows from the light one. Use it for the finished picture; the shooting stage is [exposure_bracketing](#exposure_bracketing).

entries.name: exposure_bracketing
entries.description: Several frames of the same scene shot at different exposures, usually a stop or two apart, so one of them lands or they can be combined later. Tag the set or the individual frames. Merging them is [exposure_blending](#exposure_blending).

entries.name: graduated_neutral_density
entries.description: A filter dark at the top and clear at the bottom, held over the lens to hold a bright sky back while the land keeps its exposure. Look for the transition line across the frame. For an even darkening of the whole frame, use [neutral_density_filter](#neutral_density_filter).

entries.name: highlight_rolloff
entries.description: The bright end fades gently into white instead of hitting a hard edge, so a lit cheek or a cloud keeps its shape. A quality of the medium as much as of the exposure. The hard edge is [blown_highlights](#blown_highlights).

entries.name: neutral_density_filter
entries.description: A grey filter that cuts the light evenly so a wider aperture or slower shutter can be used in bright conditions. Nothing about the tones changes, only how much light arrived. A filter graded across the frame is [graduated_neutral_density](#graduated_neutral_density).

entries.name: partial_silhouette
entries.description: The subject is nearly a dark shape but some detail is still readable in it — a lit edge, a face just visible against the sky. Use [silhouette](#silhouette) only when the shape is genuinely solid black.

entries.name: pushed_exposure
entries.description: Brightened well after the fact, in development or on the file, so the shadows are noisy and the tones a little thin. Tag the visible result, not the intention. A picture simply left dark is [underexposed](#underexposed).

entries.name: recovered_highlights
entries.description: Bright areas pulled back in processing, leaving a grey, slightly flat sky or a dull edge where full white would be expected. Look for the tell-tale dead patch. Where the recovery failed and the area is pure white, use [blown_highlights](#blown_highlights).

entries.name: shadow_detail
entries.description: The dark areas stay open and readable — fabric, hair and corners still show texture. Use it when that is the notable thing about the picture. Its absence is [crushed_blacks](#crushed_blacks).

entries.name: spot_metered
entries.description: Exposure was read from a small patch of the frame — a face, a lit hand — and the rest was left to follow. Typical of stage and [backlit](#backlit) work. For a reading of the whole frame, see [evaluative_metering](#evaluative_metering).

entries.name: tonal_banding
entries.description: Smooth gradients break into visible steps, usually across a sky or a studio backdrop, after heavy brightening or a compressed file. It is a tonal fault, not a colour cast, and shows worst in the darker half.

entries.name: tone_mapped
entries.description: The tonal range has been squeezed by software until the picture takes on halos, grey skies and unnaturally open shadows. It is the look, not the technique: a well-made [high_dynamic_range](#high_dynamic_range) picture shows none of it.

entries.name: auto_exposure_lock
entries.description: A reading was taken from one part of the scene, locked, and then the frame recomposed. The picture is still automatic, but the exposure belongs to somewhere other than what is now in the middle.

entries.name: center_weighted_metering
entries.description: The meter read the whole frame but leaned on the middle, the old default for portraits. Between [spot_metered](#spot_metered) and [evaluative_metering](#evaluative_metering) in how narrowly it looked.

entries.name: clipped_channel
entries.description: One colour channel has clipped while the others still hold detail, so a saturated red flower or a blue light loses all texture and looks like a flat patch. The picture as a whole may look fine, which is why [blown_highlights](#blown_highlights) does not cover it.

entries.name: evaluative_metering
entries.description: The camera judged exposure from the whole frame divided into zones, the usual automatic mode. Note it when the metering choice matters to how the picture turned out; otherwise [auto_exposure](#auto_exposure) is enough.

entries.name: expose_to_the_right
entries.description: Shot as bright as the highlights allow, pushing the histogram right to gather clean shadows, on the understanding that it will be pulled back later. A deliberate working method rather than a mistake, so do not also tag [overexposed](#overexposed).

entries.name: grey_card
entries.description: A neutral grey card is in the frame, or one was used to set the exposure, giving a known midtone to meter and later balance against. Usually a first frame of a set rather than a finished picture.

entries.name: incident_metering
entries.description: Exposure was measured at the subject with a handheld meter reading the light falling on it, rather than the light coming back off it. Immune to a dark or bright background, unlike [spot_metered](#spot_metered).

entries.name: sunny_16
entries.description: Exposure guessed from the old [daylight](#daylight) rule rather than a meter, with no metering at all involved. Worth tagging on film work where the settings were chosen by eye. Not to be confused with [manual_exposure](#manual_exposure), which may still follow a meter.

entries.name: zone_system
entries.description: Exposure and development planned so that chosen parts of the scene land on chosen tonal steps, the classic large-format discipline. Tag it only where the method is actually claimed, not for any careful exposure.

entries.name: bokeh
entries.description: The character of the out-of-focus areas, not merely their presence: how highlights render, how edges dissolve. Tag it when the quality of the blur is itself part of the picture. Plain background softness is [background_blur](#background_blur).

entries.name: shallow_depth_of_field
entries.description: Only a thin slice of the scene is sharp; everything nearer and farther falls away into blur. The everyday look of a fast lens wide open. Use [selective_focus](#selective_focus) when the point is which subject was chosen, and [paper_thin_depth_of_field](#paper_thin_depth_of_field) when the sharp slice is millimetres deep.

entries.name: background_blur
entries.description: Everything behind the subject is soft, whatever its character. The plain descriptive tag; reach for [bokeh](#bokeh) only when the quality of that blur is the point. Software-made blur belongs with the processing tags, not here.

entries.name: deep_focus
entries.description: Near and far are both sharp, so foreground and background read as one continuous space. Typical of a stopped-down lens or a small sensor. If the sharpness came from combining several frames, tag [focus_stacking](#focus_stacking) as well.

entries.name: bokeh_balls
entries.description: Discrete discs of light where point highlights fell out of focus — fairy lights, sun through leaves, wet street reflections. The picture is usually shot for them. Tag [creamy_bokeh](#creamy_bokeh) or [busy_bokeh](#busy_bokeh) as well when their character matters.

entries.name: creamy_bokeh
entries.description: Blur that melts smoothly, with no hard edges or doubled outlines in the background. Highlights fade at their rims rather than ending abruptly. The opposite tag is [busy_bokeh](#busy_bokeh).

entries.name: eye_focus
entries.description: Focus is placed on the eye, the standard target for portraits and animals, with the rest of the face allowed to soften. Check the near eye specifically. If the far eye is sharp and the near one is not, tag [back_focus](#back_focus).

entries.name: foreground_blur
entries.description: Something between the lens and the subject is thrown out of focus — leaves, railings, a shoulder — softening or framing the edge of the picture. Adds depth by layering. Blur behind the subject is [background_blur](#background_blur).

entries.name: missed_focus
entries.description: The sharp plane landed somewhere other than the intended subject — an ear instead of an eye, a shoulder instead of a face. A fault, not a style. Say [front_focus](#front_focus) or [back_focus](#back_focus) when the direction of the miss is clear.

entries.name: out_of_focus
entries.description: Something in the frame sits outside the sharp zone and is rendered as blur. The broad parent term for [background_blur](#background_blur), [foreground_blur](#foreground_blur) and [bokeh](#bokeh). Blur caused by movement during the exposure is not this.

entries.name: plane_of_focus
entries.description: Where in the scene sharpness actually lies is the picture's subject — a flat band of crispness running through a receding row of objects. Use it when that slice is visible as a shape. If the slice is tilted rather than parallel, tag [tilt_shift_focus](#tilt_shift_focus).

entries.name: selective_focus
entries.description: One element is picked out sharp and everything else is let go, so focus does the pointing. The choice of subject is the point, not merely the amount of blur. When the aim is to lift a subject clear of clutter, [subject_isolation](#subject_isolation) is the closer tag.

entries.name: soft_focus
entries.description: Sharp detail veiled by a bloom of [halation](#halation) while edges stay in place, so the picture reads as glowing rather than blurred. Classic for portraits and flowers. Genuinely misfocused pictures are [missed_focus](#missed_focus), not this.

entries.name: subject_isolation
entries.description: The subject is lifted clear of a cluttered setting by blur alone, with no sharp detail left to compete. Judged by how completely the surroundings dissolve. Selective_focus is about which subject was chosen; this is about how cleanly it stands out.

entries.name: tack_sharp
entries.description: The subject holds crisp detail down to eyelashes, fabric weave or fur at full size. A judgement about the subject, not about how much of the scene is sharp — that is [deep_focus](#deep_focus). Its opposite here is [missed_focus](#missed_focus).

entries.name: autofocus
entries.description: The camera chose and held focus, typically tracking a face, an eye or a moving subject through a burst. Note it when the tracking is the story — a sharp bird in flight, a runner kept crisp across frames. Its characteristic failure is [missed_focus](#missed_focus).

entries.name: back_focus
entries.description: The sharp plane fell behind the subject, so the ears or the wall are crisp and the face is not. Look for what is sharp rather than for how soft the subject is. The opposite miss is [front_focus](#front_focus).

entries.name: busy_bokeh
entries.description: Restless, distracting blur: doubled outlines, harsh-edged highlights, twigs and foliage turned to visual noise. Often unwanted. The tag for the opposite quality is [creamy_bokeh](#creamy_bokeh).

entries.name: cat_eye_bokeh
entries.description: Out-of-focus highlights that are round at the centre of the frame and lens-shaped slivers towards the corners, cut off by the barrel. Look at the corners to confirm. If the whole background rotates as well, add [swirly_bokeh](#swirly_bokeh).

entries.name: diffusion_filter
entries.description: The soft glow came from something in front of the lens — a [mist](#mist) or black-mist filter, stocking, or smeared clear filter. Highlights bloom outward while the focus itself is untouched. Use [soft_focus](#soft_focus) alone when the source of the bloom is unclear.

entries.name: entirely_out_of_focus
entries.description: Nothing in the frame is sharp; the whole picture is soft shapes and colour. Sometimes deliberate abstraction, sometimes a mistake. If a subject was meant to be sharp and only just missed, use [missed_focus](#missed_focus).

entries.name: focus_falloff
entries.description: How quickly sharpness gives way as the scene recedes: a gradual, gentle transition, or an abrupt drop just behind the subject. Tag it when that gradient is what makes the picture. The amount of blur at the far end is [background_blur](#background_blur) instead.

entries.name: focus_stacking
entries.description: Several frames focused at different distances, combined into one picture sharp from front to back. The usual answer to a macro subject that a single exposure cannot cover. Sharpness won by stopping down alone is just [deep_focus](#deep_focus).

entries.name: front_focus
entries.description: The sharp plane fell in front of the subject: the nearer edge is crisp and the intended point is soft. Common with fast lenses at close range. The opposite miss is [back_focus](#back_focus).

entries.name: hyperfocal
entries.description: Focused at the distance that pulls everything from roughly half that distance to the horizon into acceptable sharpness. The [landscape](#landscape) habit: a near rock and a far ridge both readable. Note it when the near foreground is deliberately included and sharp.

entries.name: infinity_focus
entries.description: Focus set at the far end of the scale, for stars, distant mountains or aircraft, with nothing near the camera expected to be sharp. Foreground objects, if any, are noticeably soft. When a near foreground is meant to hold up too, that is [hyperfocal](#hyperfocal).

entries.name: manual_focus
entries.description: Focus was set by hand on the lens ring rather than by the camera. Worth tagging where it shows: an adapted old lens, a deliberately odd focus point, work through glass or foliage that would defeat automation. Setting distance by scale ahead of time is [zone_focusing](#zone_focusing).

entries.name: paper_thin_depth_of_field
entries.description: The sharp slice is so shallow that an eyelash is sharp and the pupil behind it is not. Comes from very fast optics at close range or from macro work. Ordinary wide-open portraits are just [shallow_depth_of_field](#shallow_depth_of_field).

entries.name: rack_focus
entries.description: Focus is shifted from one subject to another during the shot, handing attention across the frame. A moving-picture tag; in a still it can only apply to a sequence or a frame caught mid-shift. Watch for [focus_breathing](#focus_breathing) riding along with it.

entries.name: swirly_bokeh
entries.description: Background blur that appears to rotate around the subject, the smearing growing stronger towards the frame edges. Comes from old uncorrected lens designs shot wide open. Distinct from [cat_eye_bokeh](#cat_eye_bokeh), where the highlights are merely clipped rather than swirling.

entries.name: tilt_shift_focus
entries.description: The plane of focus is tilted away from the sensor, so sharpness runs as a wedge across the scene instead of parallel to the frame. Either everything on an oblique surface is sharp, or a band cuts diagonally through the picture. A blur band painted on afterwards is not this.

entries.name: anamorphic_bokeh
entries.description: Out-of-focus highlights stretched into vertical ovals by a squeeze optic, usually alongside horizontal flare streaks. Judge it on the highlight shape, not the aspect ratio of the frame. Round highlights clipped at the corners are [cat_eye_bokeh](#cat_eye_bokeh) instead.

entries.name: bokeh_panorama
entries.description: Many frames from a long fast lens stitched into one wide picture, giving a broad view with blur far shallower than that focal length could manage alone. Look for a wide field with an implausibly dissolved background. Ordinary stitching without that effect is not this.

entries.name: circle_of_confusion
entries.description: The size a point of light grows to when it is off the sharp plane — the measure behind every depth-of-field judgement. Worth tagging on test shots and comparisons made to show it. For ordinary pictures use [shallow_depth_of_field](#shallow_depth_of_field) or [deep_focus](#deep_focus).

entries.name: donut_bokeh
entries.description: Ring-shaped out-of-focus highlights with a hole in the centre, produced by a mirror lens's central obstruction. Unmistakable once the background has any specular points. Onion_ring_bokeh has rings but no hollow core.

entries.name: focus_breathing
entries.description: The framing shifts slightly wider or tighter as focus is racked, because the lens changes its angle of view while focusing. Visible only across a sequence or a clip, never in a single still. Usually noted alongside [rack_focus](#rack_focus).

entries.name: focus_shift
entries.description: The sharp plane moved backwards as the lens was stopped down, so a shot focused wide open and taken closed is slightly off. Shows as a consistent rearward miss across a set, not a random one. A one-off error is just [missed_focus](#missed_focus).

entries.name: freelensing
entries.description: The lens is held detached and tilted in front of the camera, giving a swung plane of focus plus light leaks and edge softness. Messier and less controlled than [tilt_shift_focus](#tilt_shift_focus), which does the same thing on a proper mount.

entries.name: onion_ring_bokeh
entries.description: Highlight discs filled with concentric rings, left by the turning marks on a moulded aspherical element. Visible only on bright specular points. Not to be confused with [donut_bokeh](#donut_bokeh), which is hollow in the middle.

entries.name: shaped_bokeh
entries.description: Highlights rendered as hearts, stars or other shapes by a cut-out card held over the front of the lens. A deliberate effect, always over point highlights at night or against sparkling water. Iris blades giving pentagons or hexagons is not this — that is ordinary [bokeh_balls](#bokeh_balls).

entries.name: soap_bubble_bokeh
entries.description: Highlight discs with a bright, hard-drawn outer rim and a flat interior, like a bubble. A signature of certain undercorrected older optics. The rim is the tell; a plain bright disc is just [bokeh_balls](#bokeh_balls).

entries.name: split_diopter
entries.description: A half lens held over part of the frame puts a near and a far subject in focus at once, leaving a soft seam where the two zones meet. Look for that blurred dividing line — it is the giveaway. Both planes sharp without a seam is [focus_stacking](#focus_stacking) or [deep_focus](#deep_focus).

entries.name: zone_focusing
entries.description: The lens was set to a distance in advance and the photographer moved until the subject fell inside the sharp zone, without focusing per frame. The street habit for fast [candid](#candid) work; expect a slightly stopped-down look and occasional near misses. Focusing by eye per shot is [manual_focus](#manual_focus).

entries.name: frozen_motion
entries.description: A fast-moving subject is caught completely sharp: a splash suspended, a dancer mid-leap, dust hanging in the air. The point of the picture is that motion was stopped. Tag [flash_freeze](#flash_freeze) when a short [flash](#flash) rather than a fast shutter did the stopping.

entries.name: long_exposure
entries.description: The shutter was held open long enough for the world to move during the frame, so anything in motion smears while the static parts stay sharp. The umbrella tag for the whole family. Tag the specific look too where one fits, such as [silky_water](#silky_water) or [light_trails](#light_trails).

entries.name: motion_blur
entries.description: Something in the frame is stretched or smeared because it moved while the shutter was open. Use it whenever blur comes from movement rather than from focus. If the whole frame is smeared because the camera moved, [camera_shake](#camera_shake) or [intentional_camera_movement](#intentional_camera_movement) is the more precise tag.

entries.name: camera_shake
entries.description: The whole frame is doubled or smeared because the camera moved while the shutter was open, usually handheld at too slow a speed. An accident rather than an effect. Deliberate sweeping for an abstract result is [intentional_camera_movement](#intentional_camera_movement).

entries.name: light_trails
entries.description: Moving lights leave continuous ribbons across the frame: headlights and tail lights on a road, a passing train, a ferris wheel. The light sources themselves are the only thing recorded. A hand-carried light drawing shapes deliberately is [light_painting](#light_painting).

entries.name: panning_shot
entries.description: The camera was swung along with a moving subject during a slow exposure, leaving the subject readable and the background pulled into horizontal streaks. A picture of a moving subject that is simply smeared, with a sharp background, is [subject_blur](#subject_blur) instead.

entries.name: silky_water
entries.description: A waterfall, stream or sea surface rendered as a smooth milky veil by an exposure of a second or more. The classic reason to put a camera on a tripod in [daylight](#daylight). Sharp droplets and spray instead mean [frozen_splash](#frozen_splash).

entries.name: subject_blur
entries.description: The background and surroundings are sharp while a moving subject is smeared. The camera was held still and the shutter was simply too slow for the action. The opposite arrangement, sharp subject against a streaked background, is [panning_shot](#panning_shot).

entries.name: blurred_crowd
entries.description: Passing people are reduced to anonymous streaks or thinned almost out of the picture while the architecture stays sharp. The usual way of emptying a busy street or station. A single recognisable half-transparent person is [ghosted_figure](#ghosted_figure).

entries.name: bulb_exposure
entries.description: The shutter was held open by hand, beyond the camera's timed range, for anything from several seconds to hours. Tag it when the exposure is clearly minutes long rather than a metered second or two. Star arcs from such a frame are [star_trails](#star_trails).

entries.name: cloud_streaks
entries.description: Moving cloud drawn into soft bands or radiating streaks across the sky by a long exposure, often with a still [landscape](#landscape) or building beneath. Frequently paired with [silky_water](#silky_water) in the same frame. Point-like stars smeared into arcs are [star_trails](#star_trails).

entries.name: daytime_long_exposure
entries.description: A long exposure made in full [daylight](#daylight), so the frame is bright but moving water, cloud and people are smoothed away. Usually requires heavy filtration. Tag it alongside whatever the movement produced, such as [cloud_streaks](#cloud_streaks) or [blurred_crowd](#blurred_crowd).

entries.name: dragged_shutter
entries.description: Flash freezes the subject while a slow shutter lets ambient light and movement register as a trailing smear around it. The signature look of night events and dance floors. Without the [flash](#flash) there is no sharp core and it is simply [motion_blur](#motion_blur).

entries.name: firework_trails
entries.description: A firework burst recorded as expanding filaments of light rather than a frozen ball, because the shutter stayed open through the whole rise and fall. Often several bursts overlap in one frame. Static illuminated smoke without trails does not count.

entries.name: flash_freeze
entries.description: Motion is frozen by the brevity of a [flash](#flash) burst rather than by the shutter, usually in a darkened room where the ambient light contributes nothing. Look for the hard, even flash lighting alongside the razor-sharp action. High-speed rigs with triggers belong under [high_speed_photography](#high_speed_photography).

entries.name: foliage_blur
entries.description: Leaves, grass or branches softened into a restless smear by wind during the exposure while trunks and ground stay sharp. Often unintended in [landscape](#landscape) work and worth flagging either way. Deliberate sweeping of the whole frame is [intentional_camera_movement](#intentional_camera_movement).

entries.name: frozen_splash
entries.description: Liquid caught in mid-air as sharp droplets, sheets or a crown. Common in drink and product work and in poured-water portraits. The opposite treatment of moving water, smoothed into a soft veil by a slow shutter, is [silky_water](#silky_water).

entries.name: ghosted_figure
entries.description: A person who moved through part of a long exposure is recorded as a half-transparent shape with the scene showing through them. Common in busy interiors shot on a tripod. Where the figures dissolve away entirely into streaks, use [blurred_crowd](#blurred_crowd).

entries.name: high_speed_photography
entries.description: An event too fast for the eye is captured with specialist timing: a bursting balloon, a bullet through fruit, a crown of milk. Usually triggered by sound or a beam. Ordinary fast-shutter sports and wildlife work is just [frozen_motion](#frozen_motion).

entries.name: intentional_camera_movement
entries.description: The camera was deliberately swept, tilted or jiggled during a slow exposure to turn the whole scene into abstract streaks of colour. Nothing in the frame is sharp and that is the point. Accidental smearing from an unsteady hand is [camera_shake](#camera_shake).

entries.name: light_painting
entries.description: Someone moved a torch, sparkler or lamp through a dark scene during a long exposure, drawing shapes or brushing light onto a subject. The light source is usually invisible, only its path shows. Passing traffic and other uncontrolled lights are [light_trails](#light_trails).

entries.name: rolling_shutter_distortion
entries.description: A sensor read line by line during fast movement leans vertical edges over or bends propellers into rubbery curves. A defect rather than an effect, but distinctive. Uniform smearing without skew or bending is plain [motion_blur](#motion_blur).

entries.name: star_trails
entries.description: The night sky's rotation recorded as concentric arcs, from a single very long frame or a stacked series. Length of the arcs tells you the exposure time. Short streaks from an over-long single frame that was meant to show points still count.

entries.name: stroboscopic_motion
entries.description: Repeated flashes during one open shutter lay a sequence of separate poses across the same frame, so a swing or jump reads as a row of stepped positions. The subject appears several times, sharply, not as a smear. Continuous smearing is [motion_blur](#motion_blur).

entries.name: zoom_burst
entries.description: The zoom ring was turned during the exposure, so everything streaks outward from the centre of the frame like a starfield jump. A radial explosion of lines around a roughly sharp middle. Rotational streaking instead means [spin_blur](#spin_blur).

entries.name: camera_toss
entries.description: The camera was thrown or spun free during a long exposure, so lights in a dark scene trace loops and knots as it tumbled. Chaotic and unrepeatable. Controlled sweeping while the camera stays in hand is [intentional_camera_movement](#intentional_camera_movement).

entries.name: light_orb
entries.description: A light on a string or stick spun around a fixed point during the exposure so the trails close into a sphere or ring floating in the scene. Smooth and continuous, unlike the spark shower of [steel_wool_spin](#steel_wool_spin).

entries.name: propeller_blur
entries.description: A spinning rotor, fan or wheel drawn as a translucent disc or arc, which is what makes an aircraft or engine look alive. Deliberately chosen over freezing the blades. Blades stopped dead by a fast shutter are [frozen_motion](#frozen_motion) instead.

entries.name: slit_scan
entries.description: The frame is built up through a narrow slit while subject or film moves, so time rather than space runs across the picture; the result is smeared and unreadable as an ordinary view. Used for finish lines and photo strips. Not a post-processing warp.

entries.name: spin_blur
entries.description: The camera was rotated about the lens axis during the exposure, smearing the scene into circular arcs around the centre. Distinguish from [zoom_burst](#zoom_burst), where the streaks run outward rather than around.

entries.name: steel_wool_spin
entries.description: Burning steel wool whirled on a cable throws a sphere or arc of orange sparks across a long exposure. Instantly recognisable by the shower of bouncing spark trails. A smooth continuous ring with no sparks is more likely [light_orb](#light_orb).

entries.name: lens_flare
entries.description: Stray light from a bright source scattering inside the lens, showing as blobs, rings, streaks or a general wash. Use [ghosting](#ghosting) or [veiling_flare](#veiling_flare) for the specific forms, and this tag when flare is simply present.

entries.name: telephoto
entries.description: A long lens that crops in tight from a distance and stacks the planes of the scene together. Tag [lens_compression](#lens_compression) when that flattening is the visible effect rather than just the reach.

entries.name: vignetting
entries.description: The corners are darker than the middle, either from the lens or added afterwards to pull the eye inward. Note it whenever the falloff is plainly visible against a sky or an even wall.

entries.name: wide_angle
entries.description: Shot with a lens noticeably wider than normal vision, so a lot of the scene fits in and near things loom over far ones. Use [ultra_wide](#ultra_wide) for the extreme end, and [wide_angle_distortion](#wide_angle_distortion) when stretched edges are the point.

entries.name: barrel_distortion
entries.description: Straight lines bow outward from the centre, most obvious along the frame edges of a wide zoom. A lens fault rather than a look; the deliberate extreme version is [fisheye](#fisheye).

entries.name: chromatic_aberration
entries.description: Coloured edges where the lens fails to bring all wavelengths to the same place: green and magenta fringes along high-contrast borders, worst in the corners. For the violet halo around out-of-focus highlights use [purple_fringing](#purple_fringing).

entries.name: converging_verticals
entries.description: Upright lines lean inward or outward because the camera was tilted up or down, most visibly on buildings. Corrected in a [tilt_shift](#tilt_shift) shot or in software; leave the tag off once the walls stand straight.

entries.name: ghosting
entries.description: Discrete reflections of the aperture strung across the frame opposite a bright light, usually coloured circles or polygons. Distinct from the contrast-killing wash of [veiling_flare](#veiling_flare).

entries.name: lens_compression
entries.description: Distant planes look stacked and near the same size because the picture was taken far back with a long lens. The classic case is a huge moon or mountain behind a small subject. Its opposite is [wide_angle_distortion](#wide_angle_distortion).

entries.name: macro_lens
entries.description: Made near life size with a lens that focuses very close, showing texture the eye cannot resolve unaided. About the optics and magnification; the resulting sliver of sharpness belongs to the depth-of-field tags.

entries.name: perspective_distortion
entries.description: Shapes read wrong because of where the camera stood: a nose enlarged, a building leaning, a hand thrust forward. It comes from camera distance and angle, not from the glass, unlike [barrel_distortion](#barrel_distortion).

entries.name: standard_lens
entries.description: A normal focal length that renders roughly the perspective the eye expects: no looming foreground, no flattening. Reach for it when nothing about the geometry draws attention to itself.

entries.name: sun_star
entries.description: A bright point light drawn out into clean rays by a stopped-down aperture, typically the sun peeking past an edge or a streetlamp at night. Different from the scattered blobs of [ghosting](#ghosting).

entries.name: ultra_wide
entries.description: The extreme wide end, where walls fall away steeply and anything near the frame edge is stretched. Straight lines stay straight unless the lens is a [fisheye](#fisheye), which bends them instead.

entries.name: wide_angle_distortion
entries.description: The stretched, egg-shaped rendering of faces and objects near the edges of a wide frame, with the foreground exaggerated. Straight lines stay straight here; if they bow, tag [barrel_distortion](#barrel_distortion) or [fisheye](#fisheye).

entries.name: anamorphic_flare
entries.description: A long horizontal streak, usually blue, thrown across the frame by a bright light in a squeeze lens. Ordinary round or polygonal artefacts belong under [lens_flare](#lens_flare) or [ghosting](#ghosting) instead.

entries.name: anamorphic_look
entries.description: The wide, slightly stretched rendering of a squeeze lens: oval highlights, horizontal streaks off bright points, a cinematic frame. Tag [anamorphic_flare](#anamorphic_flare) when the streaks themselves are the feature.

entries.name: corner_softness
entries.description: Detail smears or goes mushy towards the edges while the middle stays crisp, typical of a wide lens used wide open. Tag [field_curvature](#field_curvature) instead when refocusing makes the edges sharp at the centre's expense.

entries.name: dirty_lens
entries.description: Smears, dust or fingerprints on the front element scatter light into soft blooms and streaks around highlights. Local and irregular, unlike the even wash of [veiling_flare](#veiling_flare) from a clean lens.

entries.name: fisheye
entries.description: An extremely wide lens that bends every straight line away from the centre instead of correcting it. Not the same as [barrel_distortion](#barrel_distortion), which is a fault in a lens meant to be rectilinear.

entries.name: forced_perspective
entries.description: A deliberate trick of alignment that makes something look far larger, smaller or nearer than it is, like a hand appearing to hold the sun. The effect is staged, which separates it from incidental [perspective_distortion](#perspective_distortion).

entries.name: foreshortening
entries.description: A limb, road or body seen end-on so its length collapses towards the camera. Use it when the shortening of a receding form is the striking thing, rather than the general stretching of [wide_angle_distortion](#wide_angle_distortion).

entries.name: miniature_effect
entries.description: A real scene that reads as a scale model because a tilted plane of sharpness cuts across it, usually shot down from height. Distinct from ordinary shallow depth of field, where the blur follows distance rather than a slanted band.

entries.name: one_point_perspective
entries.description: The camera faces a scene square-on so everything converges on a single central point: tunnels, aisles, symmetrical streets. Angled views with two sets of converging lines are ordinary [vanishing_point](#vanishing_point) pictures.

entries.name: optical_vignetting
entries.description: The lens itself clips light towards the corners with the aperture open, dimming them and squashing out-of-focus highlights into lemon shapes. Even, circular darkening added in editing is plain [vignetting](#vignetting).

entries.name: pincushion_distortion
entries.description: Straight lines pinch inward towards the centre, the opposite of [barrel_distortion](#barrel_distortion) and typical of the long end of a zoom. Easiest to spot on a horizon or a doorframe near the edge.

entries.name: prime_lens
entries.description: Shot on a fixed focal length, so framing came from moving the camera. A gear fact rather than a look; note it when the file or the shooter's habit makes it worth recording.

entries.name: purple_fringing
entries.description: A violet glow hugging bright edges just outside the plane of focus, common on branches against a bright sky with a fast lens wide open. A specific kind of [chromatic_aberration](#chromatic_aberration), not the lateral corner fringes.

entries.name: raindrops_on_lens
entries.description: Water sits on the front element or a filter, throwing blurred blobs and bright spots over the picture. Tag it for drops on the glass in front of the camera, not for [rain](#rain) visible in the scene itself.

entries.name: rectilinear_lens
entries.description: A wide lens that keeps straight lines straight, at the price of stretching subjects near the corners. Worth tagging on architecture and interiors where the contrast with [fisheye](#fisheye) matters.

entries.name: short_telephoto
entries.description: The mild long end used for flattering head-and-shoulders work: slightly compressed features, comfortable working distance, no obvious stacking. Distinct from [super_telephoto](#super_telephoto), which pulls in far-off subjects.

entries.name: super_telephoto
entries.description: Very long reach, the kind used for birds, wildlife and distant sport, where the subject fills the frame from far away and the background is a compressed wash. Heat shimmer and hand shake often show.

entries.name: tilt_shift
entries.description: Made with a lens that shifts or tilts off the optical axis, used to keep verticals upright or to swing the sharp plane across the scene. For the resulting narrow sharp band alone, the focus tags are more precise.

entries.name: veiling_flare
entries.description: A milky [haze](#haze) over part or all of the frame that lifts the blacks and drains contrast, with no distinct shapes. Where you can point at separate blobs of light, tag [ghosting](#ghosting) instead.

entries.name: wide_angle_close_up
entries.description: A wide lens pushed right up to the subject so the nearest part looms and the surroundings fall away behind it. Common for pets, hands, food and cars; the drama comes from distance, not magnification, unlike [macro_lens](#macro_lens).

entries.name: zoom_lens
entries.description: Shot on a variable focal length lens. Again a gear fact, not an appearance; if the zoom was turned during the exposure that is a motion effect, not this tag.

entries.name: circular_fisheye
entries.description: The [fisheye](#fisheye) variant that draws a round image inside black corners rather than filling the frame. Use plain fisheye for the full-frame kind that covers the whole rectangle.

entries.name: coma
entries.description: Point lights near the frame corners smear into little wings or comet shapes instead of staying round. Most often noticed in night and astro frames; stopping the lens down usually removes it.

entries.name: diffraction_softening
entries.description: Overall fine detail is dulled because the lens was stopped far down, so even the plane of focus is slightly hazy across the whole frame. Distinct from [corner_softness](#corner_softness), which spares the centre.

entries.name: distortion_corrected
entries.description: The picture has had its lens geometry [straightened](#straightened), in camera or afterwards, so bowed lines are flat and the corners are stretched or [cropped](#cropped). Use it when the correction itself is visible, for example a defished [fisheye](#fisheye) frame.

entries.name: field_curvature
entries.description: The sharp zone is a dish rather than a flat plane, so a flat subject cannot be sharp at the centre and the edges at once. Look for a sharp middle with soft edges that focus fixes only by trading one for the other.

entries.name: mustache_distortion
entries.description: A mixed fault where a line bows out near the centre and back in towards the corners, so it wavers rather than curving one way. Worth its own tag because simple barrel or pincushion correction cannot fix it.

entries.name: spherical_aberration
entries.description: A soft glow spreading out of bright areas because rays through the edge of the lens focus differently from those through the middle. Sharp detail survives underneath, which separates it from simple missed focus.

entries.name: centred_composition
entries.description: The subject sits squarely in the middle of the frame, usually with matching space on both sides. Common in portraits shot head-on and in architecture. It often reads as [symmetry](#symmetry), but a centred subject in an uneven setting is centred without being symmetrical.

entries.name: fill_the_frame
entries.description: The subject runs edge to edge with almost no surroundings left, so there is nothing to read but the thing itself. The opposite pole from [negative_space](#negative_space); note that this is about how much the subject occupies, not how close the lens was.

entries.name: negative_space
entries.description: Large empty areas — sky, wall, water, plain background — occupy most of the frame and set off a small subject. Use [breathing_room](#breathing_room) for a moderate margin around the subject; this tag is for emptiness that dominates.

entries.name: rule_of_thirds
entries.description: The main subject or the horizon sits about a third of the way in from an edge rather than in the middle. Use it when the placement is clearly off-centre and deliberate; if the subject is simply anywhere but the middle, [off_centre_subject](#off_centre_subject) is the looser tag.

entries.name: symmetry
entries.description: The two halves of the frame mirror each other about a vertical or horizontal axis, as in a facade shot straight on or a [reflection](#reflection) in still water. If the mirroring is only approximate and the difference is the point, use [broken_symmetry](#broken_symmetry).

entries.name: asymmetry
entries.description: Weight is distributed unevenly across the frame — a large element on one side answered by a small one, or by empty space. Use it when the imbalance is the structure; if the sides do settle into equilibrium, [balanced_composition](#balanced_composition) fits better.

entries.name: balanced_composition
entries.description: The visual weights on either side of the frame settle against each other, so nothing tips. Applies to symmetrical and asymmetrical arrangements alike. Use [visual_tension](#visual_tension) for the opposite case, where the arrangement is deliberately unsettled.

entries.name: breathing_room
entries.description: A comfortable margin of plain space around the subject so it is not pressed against the edges. Milder than [negative_space](#negative_space), which dominates the frame, and the opposite of [fill_the_frame](#fill_the_frame).

entries.name: diagonal_composition
entries.description: The main lines run corner to corner rather than with the frame edges, giving the picture a slant and a sense of movement. It concerns what is in the frame, not a tilted camera — for a tipped horizon use the viewpoint tag instead.

entries.name: layered_composition
entries.description: Distinct planes stack from near to far — something close, the subject, and a background — so the frame reads as deep. Use [foreground_interest](#foreground_interest) when only the near plane is deliberate, and [horizontal_bands](#horizontal_bands) when the divisions are flat stripes rather than depth.

entries.name: lone_subject
entries.description: One small figure or object alone in a large frame, with nothing else competing for attention. About arrangement, not lens or focus — for a subject separated by blur, use the focus tags instead.

entries.name: minimalist_composition
entries.description: Very few elements, plain surroundings and a lot of nothing, reduced until only the essential shape remains. Where [negative_space](#negative_space) describes the empty area, this describes the whole approach; the two usually go together.

entries.name: off_centre_subject
entries.description: The subject is placed away from the middle, with the remaining space doing the work. The general case of [rule_of_thirds](#rule_of_thirds); use this when the placement is clearly off to one side but does not sit on a thirds line.

entries.name: broken_pattern
entries.description: A regular repeat with one element missing, tilted, or a different colour, and that interruption is the picture. Distinct from [broken_symmetry](#broken_symmetry), which breaks a mirror rather than a series.

entries.name: broken_symmetry
entries.description: An otherwise mirrored arrangement with one element out of place, and that odd element is what the picture is about. Tag it alongside [symmetry](#symmetry) only when the break is deliberate; a merely sloppy near-symmetry is not this.

entries.name: cluttered_composition
entries.description: Too many competing elements and no clear path for the eye, whether by accident or as the point of the picture. The opposite of [minimalist_composition](#minimalist_composition); use [fill_the_frame](#fill_the_frame) when one subject fills it rather than many.

entries.name: figure_ground_separation
entries.description: The subject stands clear of its background by shape, tone or colour, with no merging edges or poles growing out of heads. Tag it when the separation is the notable thing; it is a compositional decision, not a depth-of-field one.

entries.name: golden_ratio
entries.description: The frame is divided at roughly 1:1.618 rather than into equal thirds, putting the subject slightly nearer the centre than [rule_of_thirds](#rule_of_thirds) would. Only tag it when the proportion is evidently the plan, not for any pleasing off-centre placement.

entries.name: grid_composition
entries.description: The frame is filled with a regular rectangular array — windows on a facade, tiles, shelved goods — and the grid itself is the structure. Related to [repetition](#repetition), but here the units line up in rows and columns rather than merely recurring.

entries.name: headroom
entries.description: The space left between the top of a head and the top edge of the frame. Worth tagging when it is conspicuous — a lot of empty sky above, or a crown clipped by the edge. For space in front of a gaze, use [lead_room](#lead_room).

entries.name: high_horizon
entries.description: The horizon or the main dividing line sits near the top of the frame, giving most of the picture to the ground, water or floor. The counterpart of [low_horizon](#low_horizon); a horizon across the middle usually reads as [centred_composition](#centred_composition).

entries.name: horizontal_bands
entries.description: The picture reads as stacked strips across the frame: sand, sea and sky, or field, treeline and cloud. Use it when the horizontal division carries the picture; where the bands sit in depth rather than in stripes, use [layered_composition](#layered_composition).

entries.name: lead_room
entries.description: Space left on the side the subject faces or moves toward, so a look or a stride has somewhere to go. Its absence, with the subject pressed against the edge it faces, usually reads as [visual_tension](#visual_tension).

entries.name: low_horizon
entries.description: The horizon sits near the bottom of the frame and sky fills most of the picture. Often paired with [negative_space](#negative_space) when the sky is plain. The counterpart of [high_horizon](#high_horizon).

entries.name: overlapping_forms
entries.description: Shapes cross in front of one another so the order of depth is legible without any blur or perspective cue. Use it when the overlap is doing the structural work; if the planes are clearly separated, [layered_composition](#layered_composition) is closer.

entries.name: radial_composition
entries.description: Lines or elements fan outward from a single point like spokes — sunbeams, a fan vault, cutlery laid around a plate. If the spokes repeat evenly all the way round, [radial_symmetry](#radial_symmetry) is the stronger tag.

entries.name: radial_symmetry
entries.description: The picture repeats around a centre point rather than across an axis: a dome from below, a spiral staircase, a wheel. Distinct from [radial_composition](#radial_composition), where lines merely fan outward without the [repetition](#repetition) being regular.

entries.name: rule_of_odds
entries.description: An odd number of subjects — three, five — so the eye settles on a middle one instead of splitting between pairs. Tag it when the count is clearly the arrangement; with exactly three placed apart, [triangular_composition](#triangular_composition) may also apply.

entries.name: s_curve
entries.description: A single line winds through the frame in a lazy S — a river, a path, a shoreline, a reclining figure. A more specific case of [leading_lines](#leading_lines); use that when the line is straight or simply bent once.

entries.name: spiral_composition
entries.description: Elements coil inward or outward from a centre, as in a stairwell shot down or a shell. Use [golden_spiral](#golden_spiral) only when the coil follows the golden proportion; this tag covers any spiral arrangement.

entries.name: triangular_composition
entries.description: The main elements sit at the corners of a triangle, or a broad mass narrows toward the top — a seated group, a mountain, a pyramid of objects. Read as stable and settled, unlike [diagonal_composition](#diagonal_composition), which reads as movement.

entries.name: visual_tension
entries.description: The arrangement is deliberately unsettled: a subject crowded against an edge, a heavy mass with nothing answering it, elements about to collide. The counterpart of [balanced_composition](#balanced_composition), and usually a reason to reach for [asymmetry](#asymmetry) as well.

entries.name: golden_spiral
entries.description: The eye is led along a widening spiral that tightens onto the subject, often built from a shell, a staircase or a curve of road. Use [spiral_composition](#spiral_composition) for any spiral arrangement; reserve this for one that actually follows the golden proportion.

entries.name: centered_composition
entries.description: The subject sits squarely in the middle of the frame and the placement is clearly deliberate, not a snapshot accident. Works with [symmetry](#symmetry), portraits shot head-on, and single objects on plain ground. An off-middle placement is [off_center_subject](#off_center_subject).

entries.name: leading_lines
entries.description: A road, fence, railing or shoreline runs into the frame and pulls the eye toward the subject. The line only has to be readable as a line; it need not be straight. Where those lines shrink toward a common point in the distance, [converging_lines](#converging_lines) or [vanishing_point](#vanishing_point) says more.

entries.name: pattern
entries.description: A regular arrangement fills the frame edge to edge and the picture is largely about that regularity — tiles, scales, brickwork, a packed crowd. If one element breaks the run, add [broken_pattern](#broken_pattern). A few scattered repeats are [repetition](#repetition).

entries.name: reflection
entries.description: A reflective surface carries a second image of the scene and is part of what the picture is about. The umbrella tag; add [water_reflection](#water_reflection), [mirror_reflection](#mirror_reflection) or [window_reflection](#window_reflection) where one fits. Small bright specular points on a surface are a lighting matter, not this.

entries.name: clean_background
entries.description: The subject stands against an uncluttered surface — a plain wall, open sky, still water — with nothing behind it competing for attention. This is about what was chosen or arranged, not about lens blur. Blur doing the separating belongs with the focus tags.

entries.name: converging_lines
entries.description: Parallel edges in the scene — rails, kerbs, a corridor's walls — visibly narrow toward each other as they recede. Use it for the wedge shape itself, whether or not the meeting point is inside the frame. If it is inside the frame and obvious, add [vanishing_point](#vanishing_point).

entries.name: foreground_interest
entries.description: Something deliberately placed close to the camera — rocks, flowers, a wall, a figure — gives the picture a near plane and a sense of depth. Common in [landscape](#landscape) work. If there are several distinct planes back to the horizon, [layered_composition](#layered_composition) says more.

entries.name: frame_within_a_frame
entries.description: A doorway, window, arch, branch or mirror surrounds the subject and boxes it in inside the picture. The inner frame does not have to be complete — two edges are enough. Where the near element blocks rather than surrounds, use [shooting_through](#shooting_through).

entries.name: geometric_composition
entries.description: The picture is built from plain shapes — rectangles, circles, hard angles — and reads as an arrangement of forms before it reads as a subject. Typical of architecture and graphic street work. If the shapes repeat regularly across the frame, [pattern](#pattern) is the closer tag.

entries.name: juxtaposition
entries.description: Two unrelated things are placed side by side so the pairing makes the point — old against new, an advert against the person beneath it, rich against poor. The meaning comes from the neighbouring, not from either half. Pairing purely to show size is [scale_reference](#scale_reference).

entries.name: off_center_subject
entries.description: The subject is placed away from the middle, leaving open space on one side of the frame. The umbrella tag for any off-middle placement; add [rule_of_thirds](#rule_of_thirds) when it lands on the thirds. Space left specifically in front of a moving or looking subject is a framing choice, not this.

entries.name: repetition
entries.description: The same element recurs several times across the frame — windows, chairs, gestures, columns. A handful of copies is enough; it need not be regular. Once it covers the surface as a regular texture of its own, [pattern](#pattern) is the tag.

entries.name: shooting_through
entries.description: The lens looks past something close to it — leaves, a fence, a crowd, glass, a gap — so part of the frame is veiled or blocked. Often the near element is out of focus. When that element neatly surrounds the subject instead, it is [frame_within_a_frame](#frame_within_a_frame).

entries.name: vanishing_point
entries.description: The point where receding parallels meet is visible in the picture and acts as its anchor, usually at the end of a street, tunnel or track. Tag it only when that point is in frame. Lines that merely narrow off toward the edge are [converging_lines](#converging_lines).

entries.name: water_reflection
entries.description: A lake, river, puddle or wet pavement doubles the scene above it. Often paired with a horizon through the middle for a mirrored frame. Reflections in glass belong to [window_reflection](#window_reflection).

entries.name: busy_background
entries.description: Signs, branches, poles or bystanders pile up behind the subject and pull at the eye. Tag it when the clutter is a visible feature of the picture, whether deliberate or a fault. The opposite arrangement is [clean_background](#clean_background).

entries.name: centered_horizon
entries.description: The horizon cuts the frame across the middle, splitting it into two equal bands. Usually deliberate, and usually paired with a [reflection](#reflection). If the split is uneven, [low_horizon](#low_horizon) or [high_horizon](#high_horizon) describes it better.

entries.name: diminishing_perspective
entries.description: The same thing repeats into the distance and gets smaller each time — lamp posts, arches, pylons, a row of boats. The shrinking sizes are what carry the depth. Use [repetition](#repetition) instead when the copies stay the same size across a flat surface.

entries.name: mirror_reflection
entries.description: A mirror in the scene shows the subject, the photographer, or something outside the direct view. Useful for pictures that hold two viewpoints at once. A shot made of oneself in a mirror is better described by the [portrait](#portrait) genre tags; use this for the device.

entries.name: rhythm
entries.description: Repeating elements are spaced so they set a beat across the frame, often with gaps or size changes giving it a cadence. Arches, pillars, waves, footprints. Where the repeats are flat and even with no such pulse, tag [pattern](#pattern).

entries.name: scale_reference
entries.description: Something of known size — a person, a car, a doorway — is included so the viewer can read how big the rest is. Standard in [landscape](#landscape), architecture and macro work. If the sizes are being faked rather than reported, it is [forced_perspective](#forced_perspective).

entries.name: texture_study
entries.description: The picture is about a surface — rust, bark, fabric, peeling paint, sand — filling the frame with no subject beyond the material itself. Often shot flat-on in raking light. If the surface resolves into a regular repeat, add [pattern](#pattern).

entries.name: window_reflection
entries.description: A shop front, car window or glass facade layers a reflected street over what is behind the glass, so two scenes overlap in one frame. A staple of street work. Where the glass is merely something the lens shoots past, use [shooting_through](#shooting_through).

entries.name: tangent
entries.description: Two edges just touch or barely graze each other — a head grazing a roofline, a pole growing out of a shoulder — and the contact flattens the depth awkwardly. Nearly always a fault worth marking. A clear overlap that reads properly is [overlapping_forms](#overlapping_forms).

entries.name: two_point_perspective
entries.description: The camera looks at a corner, so two faces of a building or object recede toward separate points near the frame's edges. Common in architecture shot from street level. A square-on view with one central meeting point is [one_point_perspective](#one_point_perspective).

entries.name: eye_level
entries.description: The camera sits at the height of the subject's eyes and points more or less level. The most neutral position there is, so it is worth tagging only when the height is deliberate. Use [high_angle](#high_angle) or [low_angle](#low_angle) when the camera is clearly above or below.

entries.name: front_view
entries.description: The camera faces the front of the subject, so a person looks toward the lens and an object shows its face. Turn the subject a little and it becomes [three_quarter_view](#three_quarter_view); a full ninety degrees is [profile_view](#profile_view).

entries.name: high_angle
entries.description: The camera is above the subject and tilted down, showing more floor or ground than sky. Covers everything from a slightly raised [portrait](#portrait) to a shot down a stairwell; reserve [bird's_eye_view](#bird's_eye_view) for a genuinely lofty vantage and [overhead_shot](#overhead_shot) for straight down.

entries.name: low_angle
entries.description: The camera is below the subject and tilted up, so the subject looms and the background falls away to sky or ceiling. Tag the extreme version, taken from the ground looking almost straight up, as [worm's_eye_view](#worm's_eye_view) instead.

entries.name: overhead_shot
entries.description: The camera points straight down at the subject, so the frame reads as a plan of the surface below. Common over tables, desks and hands at work. A merely high, angled view is [high_angle](#high_angle) or [bird's_eye_view](#bird's_eye_view).

entries.name: three_quarter_view
entries.description: The subject is turned roughly forty-five degrees to the lens, showing one side and part of the front, with the far cheek or edge just visible. The standard flattering [portrait](#portrait) position between [front_view](#front_view) and [profile_view](#profile_view).

entries.name: aerial_view
entries.description: The camera is airborne, above rooftops and trees, whether from an aircraft or a flown camera. The ground reads as a map or a [pattern](#pattern). A view from a tower or hillside is [elevated_viewpoint](#elevated_viewpoint), not this.

entries.name: bird's_eye_view
entries.description: A view from far above the subject, high enough that people and cars read as small shapes on a plane. It may still be oblique rather than straight down; when the lens points vertically at the ground use [overhead_shot](#overhead_shot).

entries.name: dutch_angle
entries.description: The camera is deliberately rolled so the horizon runs on a diagonal, tipping the whole frame. It is a stylistic choice, usually for unease or energy; an accidental slope that was meant to be level is [crooked_horizon](#crooked_horizon).

entries.name: elevated_viewpoint
entries.description: The photographer stood somewhere higher than the scene — a balcony, a wall, a flight of steps, a ladder — and shot down into it. Says where the camera was; for the framing itself use [high_angle](#high_angle), and for real altitude [aerial_view](#aerial_view).

entries.name: ground_level
entries.description: The camera rests on or just above the ground, so the surface runs away in the foreground and the horizon sits low. Use it for a level shot from down there; if the lens is also tilted steeply up, add [worm's_eye_view](#worm's_eye_view).

entries.name: over_the_shoulder
entries.description: The camera sits behind and beside one person, so their shoulder and the back of their head frame whatever they are facing. Says who we are standing with; the answering view from the other side is [reverse_angle](#reverse_angle).

entries.name: point_of_view_shot
entries.description: The camera stands where a person's eyes would be, so the picture is what they see, sometimes with their own hands or feet in frame. Distinct from [over_the_shoulder](#over_the_shoulder), which still shows the person from outside.

entries.name: profile_view
entries.description: The camera is at ninety degrees to the subject, giving a pure side view: one eye, one ear, the outline of the nose. If any of the far side of the face shows, it is a [three_quarter_view](#three_quarter_view).

entries.name: rear_view
entries.description: The camera is behind the subject, showing the back of the head or the far side of an object. Anonymous by nature and often used for a figure walking away; if a shoulder frames another subject, use [over_the_shoulder](#over_the_shoulder).

entries.name: selfie_angle
entries.description: The camera is held at arm's length by the person in the picture, typically raised a little and tipped down, with the arm sometimes visible. Describes the position; whether the result is a [portrait](#portrait) is a separate matter.

entries.name: straight_on
entries.description: The camera axis is square and perpendicular to the subject's plane, so a wall, page or shopfront shows no converging edges. About the geometry rather than which side faces us, which is [front_view](#front_view); a slanted plane is [oblique_view](#oblique_view).

entries.name: animal_eye_level
entries.description: The camera is lowered to the eye height of a small animal or a small child, meeting them levelly instead of looking down at them. Use [knee_level](#knee_level) or [ground_level](#ground_level) when the height is stated rather than the subject's eyeline.

entries.name: back_three_quarter_view
entries.description: The camera sits behind and to one side, so the subject is seen mostly from the back with a sliver of cheek or profile. Between [rear_view](#rear_view) and [profile_view](#profile_view), and the usual position for a glance over the shoulder.

entries.name: chest_level
entries.description: The camera sits at the photographer's chest, a little below eye level, softening a downward look without becoming a [low_angle](#low_angle). Often the natural height of a camera on a strap or of a phone held in both hands.

entries.name: crooked_horizon
entries.description: The camera was not held level and the horizon or verticals lean by a degree or two, plainly by accident. Tag a deliberate, decisive tilt as [dutch_angle](#dutch_angle) instead; this one is a fault worth flagging for straightening.

entries.name: forty_five_degree_angle
entries.description: The camera looks down at about forty-five degrees, the way a seated person sees a plate or a desk. A staple of food and tabletop work, sitting between [straight_on](#straight_on) and [overhead_shot](#overhead_shot).

entries.name: held_overhead
entries.description: The camera is raised above the photographer's head, usually at arm's length, to shoot over a crowd or a barrier. The angle is mildly downward and the framing is often approximate because the finder cannot be seen.

entries.name: knee_level
entries.description: The camera is roughly knee high, well under adult eye level but clear of the floor. Common for photographing children, dogs and low furniture without the exaggeration of a [ground_level](#ground_level) shot.

entries.name: oblique_view
entries.description: A flat subject — a page, a sign, a screen, a facade — photographed from a slant rather than square to it, so its edges converge and one end is nearer. Not a style choice; contrast with [straight_on](#straight_on).

entries.name: reverse_angle
entries.description: The camera has moved to the opposite side of a conversation or a scene, showing what the previous position was looking at. Only meaningful as one of a pair; commonly the answering frame to an [over_the_shoulder](#over_the_shoulder).

entries.name: shot_from_the_hip
entries.description: The camera is fired from waist height without looking through it, so the framing is loose and the horizon often askew. Tag deliberate low-held composition as [waist_level](#waist_level); this one is about the guesswork.

entries.name: waist_level
entries.description: The camera is held at waist or hip height and pointed level, the classic position for a twin-lens or a discreet street frame. Deliberate composition, unlike [shot_from_the_hip](#shot_from_the_hip), where the frame is not checked at all.

entries.name: worm's_eye_view
entries.description: An extreme low viewpoint, the camera almost on the ground looking steeply up so the subject towers overhead. Ordinary low shots belong under [low_angle](#low_angle); if the camera is simply resting on the floor but pointing level, use [ground_level](#ground_level).

entries.name: oblique_aerial
entries.description: An airborne view taken at a slant, so the horizon or the sky is visible and buildings show their faces as well as their roofs. The opposite arrangement, lens pointing vertically down, is an [overhead_shot](#overhead_shot) from the air.

entries.name: underside_view
entries.description: The camera is directly beneath the subject, looking at its underside — through a glass table, up at a bridge deck, under a leaf. Stronger than [worm's_eye_view](#worm's_eye_view), which still shows the subject from the side.

entries.name: upside_down_camera
entries.description: The body is inverted so the lens sits at the very bottom, letting it get closer to the ground or to a surface than the camera's own height allows. The picture is righted afterwards; the giveaway is a viewpoint lower than seems possible.

entries.name: black_and_white
entries.description: The picture carries no colour at all, only greys from black to white. Use this whether it was shot that way or converted afterwards. If a single tint has been laid over the greys, use [sepia](#sepia) or [toned_monochrome](#toned_monochrome) instead.

entries.name: desaturated
entries.description: Colour pulled well down but not removed, leaving pale, greyish hues. Use it where you can still name the colours; where you cannot, the picture is [black_and_white](#black_and_white). A gentler reduction that keeps colours pleasant is [muted_colours](#muted_colours).

entries.name: saturated_colours
entries.description: Strong, deep colour with plenty of punch, whether from the scene or the grade. Reach for it when the colour is the first thing you notice. Where saturation has clearly gone too far and hues turn solid or garish, use [oversaturated](#oversaturated).

entries.name: bright_and_airy
entries.description: Light, clean, slightly warm colour with soft pale tones throughout, the standard wedding and lifestyle treatment. It is the colour look, not the exposure — for the tonal version use [high_key](#high_key). Its counterpart is [moody_grade](#moody_grade).

entries.name: colour_cast
entries.description: An unwanted tint over the whole picture from a wrong white balance or a coloured surface nearby — greenish under fluorescent tubes, blue in shade. It reads as an error, not a choice; a deliberate shift is [warm_grade](#warm_grade) or [cool_grade](#cool_grade).

entries.name: colour_graded
entries.description: The colour has visibly been worked on rather than left as shot — hues shifted, a look applied, a mood imposed. Use it as the general tag when the specific look has no better name of its own.

entries.name: complementary_colours
entries.description: Two opposing hues carrying the frame — orange against blue, red against green, yellow against purple — so each makes the other look stronger. The graded blockbuster version of the orange-blue pair has its own tag, [teal_and_orange](#teal_and_orange).

entries.name: cool_grade
entries.description: Colour pushed towards blue and cyan, giving a cold, clinical or night-time feel. A deliberate treatment rather than a wrong white balance, which is [colour_cast](#colour_cast). Cool shadows with warm highlights instead is [split_toning](#split_toning).

entries.name: dominant_colour
entries.description: One hue clearly rules the frame while other colours remain visible around it — a red coat in a grey street, a green wall behind a subject. Where almost nothing else has colour at all, use [monochromatic_palette](#monochromatic_palette).

entries.name: earth_tones
entries.description: A palette of browns, ochres, rusts, olives and warm greys, the colours of soil, wood and stone. Common in autumn scenes, interiors and clothing. A seasonal version dominated by red and gold foliage is [autumn_palette](#autumn_palette).

entries.name: faded_colours
