entries.description: Colours that look aged and drained, often with a warm or yellow shift, as though the print sat in a drawer for years. Applies to a grade imitating the effect as much as to a real old picture. Bleached by [daylight](#daylight) specifically is [sun_bleached](#sun_bleached).

entries.name: limited_palette
entries.description: The whole picture built from two or three colours and nothing else, whether by chance or by grading. Deliberately narrow rather than merely quiet. A single hue is [monochromatic_palette](#monochromatic_palette); a specific opposing pair is [complementary_colours](#complementary_colours).

entries.name: matte_grade
entries.description: A soft, filmic grade where the colours sit in a narrow range and the picture reads as printed on matte paper rather than glossy. Usually paired with a slight warm or green shift. This is the colour half of the look; the raised shadows themselves are [lifted_blacks](#lifted_blacks).

entries.name: monochromatic_palette
entries.description: A colour picture built almost entirely from one hue and its shades — a blue room, a field of greens. Colour is present, so this is not [black_and_white](#black_and_white). Where one colour merely leads and others answer it, use [dominant_colour](#dominant_colour).

entries.name: moody_grade
entries.description: Dark, heavy colour — deep shadows, cool or green-tinged midtones, restrained saturation — chosen to set a sombre mood. Describes the treatment, not the exposure. The opposite treatment is [bright_and_airy](#bright_and_airy).

entries.name: muted_colours
entries.description: Quiet, restrained colour — nothing shouts, but everything is clearly coloured. Often the look of overcast light or a soft grade. Stronger reduction reads as [desaturated](#desaturated); pale and light rather than merely quiet is [pastel_palette](#pastel_palette).

entries.name: neutral_grade
entries.description: Colour left true: white things are white, skin looks like skin, no hue leans one way. Worth tagging for product, reproduction and documentary work where accuracy is the point. Anything leaning warm or cool goes to [warm_grade](#warm_grade) or [cool_grade](#cool_grade).

entries.name: oversaturated
entries.description: Saturation pushed past what the picture can hold: skin turns orange, skies go electric, red flowers lose all their detail. It is a judgement about excess, not just intensity — deliberate strong colour is [saturated_colours](#saturated_colours).

entries.name: pastel_palette
entries.description: Pale, light, milky colours — powder blue, blush, mint — with nothing dark or heavy in the frame. Light as well as gentle. Quiet colour that is still normally bright is [muted_colours](#muted_colours).

entries.name: sepia
entries.description: Monochrome tinted warm brown, the old-photograph look. Reserve it for a genuinely brown tone across the whole picture, not for any warm grade. A brown-and-cream picture that still has other hues in it is [warm_grade](#warm_grade) or [faded_colours](#faded_colours).

entries.name: warm_grade
entries.description: Colour pushed deliberately towards amber and gold across the picture, for a cosy or nostalgic feel. Chosen, not accidental — an unintended warm tint is [colour_cast](#colour_cast). The brown monochrome version is [sepia](#sepia).

entries.name: analogous_colours
entries.description: Neighbouring hues used together — yellow through orange into red, or green into teal into blue — so the picture feels harmonious rather than tense. Opposing hues instead are [complementary_colours](#complementary_colours); one hue alone is [monochromatic_palette](#monochromatic_palette).

entries.name: autumn_palette
entries.description: Reds, oranges, golds and browns together, the colour scheme of falling leaves. Use it for the palette whatever the season — a grade can produce it indoors. The muddier, less fiery version is [earth_tones](#earth_tones).

entries.name: bleach_bypass
entries.description: Harsh contrast with the colour half drained away, so the picture looks silvery and metallic while still carrying some hue. A gritty, cold look for war and crime work. Even drainage without the contrast is [desaturated](#desaturated).

entries.name: colour_pop
entries.description: One subject left in colour while everything else is drained to grey. An editing effect, usually obvious at a glance. A picture that simply has one strong colour in it is [dominant_colour](#dominant_colour), not this.

entries.name: colourised
entries.description: A picture that was monochrome and has been given colour afterwards, by hand or by software. Look for flat, slightly wrong skin and clothing colour over old grain. Painted-on colour with visible brush edges is [hand_tinted](#hand_tinted).

entries.name: duotone
entries.description: The whole tonal range mapped onto two colours, typically a dark one in the shadows and a bright one in the highlights. Common in posters and covers. One tint only is [toned_monochrome](#toned_monochrome); a smooth multi-colour ramp is [gradient_map](#gradient_map).

entries.name: flat_grade
entries.description: Deliberately low-contrast, low-saturation colour left ready for grading, the way a log or flat picture profile records it. Everything looks washed and greyish but intact. For the tonal side of flatness alone, use [flat_tones](#flat_tones).

entries.name: green_cast
entries.description: A specifically green tint over the picture, the usual signature of fluorescent tubes, LED panels or light bouncing off foliage. Skin looks unwell. For a tint of any other colour use [colour_cast](#colour_cast).

entries.name: inverted_colours
entries.description: Every hue and tone [flipped](#flipped) to its opposite, so the picture reads as a negative: white hair, orange sky, black snow. An effect, applied on purpose. A true photographic negative belongs with the analogue tags instead.

entries.name: jewel_tones
entries.description: Deep, rich, saturated colour named after gemstones — emerald, sapphire, ruby, amethyst. Dark and luxurious rather than bright. The bright, hard version of strong colour is [neon_palette](#neon_palette) or [primary_colours](#primary_colours).

entries.name: mixed_white_balance
entries.description: Two light sources of different colour in one frame, so part of the picture is warm orange and part cold blue — a lamp-lit room against a window at dusk. No single white balance can fix it. A uniform tint is [colour_cast](#colour_cast).

entries.name: neon_palette
entries.description: Electric pinks, cyans, purples and greens, the colour scheme of a lit-up night street. It describes the colours in the picture, not the light sources — for the tubes themselves use [neon_light](#neon_light).

entries.name: primary_colours
entries.description: Flat, bold red, yellow and blue carrying the frame, often against white or black. A graphic, poster-like palette. Where the pairing is a colour and its opposite rather than the primaries, use [complementary_colours](#complementary_colours).

entries.name: split_toning
entries.description: Shadows and highlights pushed towards different hues while the midtones stay put — cool shadows against warm highlights is the classic pair. Subtler than [duotone](#duotone), which recolours everything. A single tint over the whole range is [toned_monochrome](#toned_monochrome).

entries.name: sun_bleached
entries.description: Colour burnt out by strong [daylight](#daylight) — pale sand, chalky walls, a whitish [haze](#haze) over everything. Warm and bright rather than merely old-looking. Aged or drained colour without the glare is [faded_colours](#faded_colours).

entries.name: teal_and_orange
entries.description: Skin and highlights pushed warm orange while shadows and backgrounds go teal, the standard modern film-poster grade. Recognisable and heavy-handed. The general principle behind it is [complementary_colours](#complementary_colours).

entries.name: toned_monochrome
entries.description: A single-colour image where the greys carry one tint throughout — cold blue, warm brown, selenium purple. The picture reads as [black_and_white](#black_and_white) with a colour laid over it. [sepia](#sepia) is the common warm case; [duotone](#duotone) maps two colours instead of one.

entries.name: false_colour
entries.description: Colours that stand for something other than what the eye would see — infrared foliage rendered pink, thermal or scientific data mapped to a colour scale. The colour carries information. An arbitrary artistic recolouring is [gradient_map](#gradient_map).

entries.name: gradient_map
entries.description: Brightness replaced by a colour ramp, so shadows, midtones and highlights each take their own hue. The result often looks unnatural and poster-like. With just two stops it is a [duotone](#duotone); a subtler version applied only to the ends is [split_toning](#split_toning).

entries.name: hand_tinted
entries.description: Colour brushed onto a monochrome print by hand — soft pink cheeks, a coloured dress, greys everywhere else. The colour sits slightly off the edges it belongs to. Digital or automatic recolouring is [colourised](#colourised).

entries.name: posterised_colour
entries.description: Colour reduced to a few flat steps, so gradients break into hard-edged bands of solid hue. A deliberate graphic effect. Faint unintended steps in a smooth sky are [tonal_banding](#tonal_banding), not this.

entries.name: film_photography
entries.description: The picture was made on photographic film rather than a digital sensor. Look for grain, edge markings, or the way a negative renders highlights. Add a format tag such as [35mm_film](#35mm_film), [medium_format_film](#medium_format_film) or [large_format_film](#large_format_film) when the size is known.

entries.name: 35mm_film
entries.description: Shot on the standard perforated 35mm strip, the format most snapshot and street work was made on. Frames are roughly 3:2 with perforations along both edges. For the wider frames of a rollfilm camera use [medium_format_film](#medium_format_film).

entries.name: black_and_white_film
entries.description: Shot on black and white stock rather than converted afterwards, so grain structure and the darkening of reds give it away. Edge markings and rebate often confirm it. A digital conversion is not this tag, even with grain added.

entries.name: film_grain
entries.description: Visible clumps of silver or dye giving the picture its texture, coarser with faster stock and bigger enlargements. Judge it in flat midtones and skies. Digital sensor noise is finer and more regular, and does not belong here.

entries.name: color_negative_film
entries.description: Shot on colour negative stock: wide latitude, gentle highlight rolloff and an orange base visible in the rebate. Scans usually sit low in contrast until corrected. Positive transparencies belong under [slide_film](#slide_film).

entries.name: darkroom_print
entries.description: A print made under an enlarger on light-sensitive paper and processed in trays, not from an inkjet or a lab machine. Look for paper texture, warm or cool blacks and hand-finished edges. Hand-coated chemistries have their own tags.

entries.name: dust_and_scratches
entries.description: White or black specks and fine lines left by dust on the negative and by scratches from the camera or the lab. They sit on top of the picture and ignore what it shows. Chemical streaks and tidelines are [developing_marks](#developing_marks).

entries.name: faded_print
entries.description: An old photographic print whose dyes have shifted and weakened, usually towards magenta or yellow with washed-out shadows. The damage belongs to the object, not to the exposure. Colour drift on the film itself is [expired_film](#expired_film).

entries.name: film_border
entries.description: The scan keeps the unexposed edge around the frame, black on a printed negative or clear on a transparency, often carrying [edge_markings](#edge_markings). A deliberate sign that this came off a strip. The white margin of a self-developing print is [instant_film](#instant_film).

entries.name: film_scan
entries.description: A digital file made from a negative or transparency, whether on a flatbed, a dedicated scanner or a camera rig. Expect inverted and corrected colour, and sometimes a visible [film_border](#film_border). A photograph of a paper print is not this.

entries.name: halation
entries.description: A soft red or orange bloom hugging bright points and edges, caused by light bouncing back through the film base. Most obvious around lamps and windows on colour negative stock. Lens flare streaks across the frame; this stays on the highlight.

entries.name: instant_film
entries.description: A self-developing print that came out of the camera finished, usually with a thick white border and one wider edge. Colours are soft and slightly shifted. For the older kind where a paper negative is peeled away, use [peel_apart_film](#peel_apart_film).

entries.name: light_leak
entries.description: Stray light reached the film through a bad seal or an opened back, burning a coloured streak or blob into part of the frame, usually running off one edge. It often repeats across neighbouring frames. An even overall veil is [fogged_film](#fogged_film).

entries.name: medium_format_film
entries.description: Shot on unperforated rollfilm, giving square or near-square frames noticeably larger than [35mm_film](#35mm_film). Grain is finer and tones smoother at the same print size. Single sheets loaded one at a time are [large_format_film](#large_format_film) instead.

entries.name: slide_film
entries.description: Shot on colour reversal stock, which gives a positive image on a clear base. Saturated colour, punchy contrast and highlights that clip abruptly. Exposure had to be exact, and unlike [color_negative_film](#color_negative_film) there is nothing to recover.

entries.name: contact_print
entries.description: The negative was laid straight onto the paper and exposed, so the print is exactly negative size and extremely sharp. Standard for [large_format_film](#large_format_film) and most hand-coated processes. A whole roll proofed this way is a [contact_sheet](#contact_sheet).

entries.name: contact_sheet
entries.description: A whole roll printed frame by frame at negative size on one sheet, used for choosing and marking edits. Grease-pencil crops, ticks and frame numbers are typical. A single frame printed the same way is [contact_print](#contact_print).

entries.name: cross_processing
entries.description: Film developed in the wrong chemistry, slide stock in negative process or the reverse, giving skewed colour, blocked shadows and hard contrast. The cast is strong and consistent through the roll. A digital grade imitating it is not this.

entries.name: date_stamp
entries.description: An orange or yellow date burned into a corner of the frame by the camera's data back. A strong marker of amateur snapshot film. A date added later in software, or handwritten on the print, is not this.

entries.name: deckled_border
entries.description: The paper print keeps its white margin, often with a scalloped or serrated edge cut by a lab trimmer, sometimes with a date or lab code along it. A quick marker of a vintage snapshot. The border of a self-developing print is [instant_film](#instant_film).

entries.name: developing_marks
entries.description: Streaks, tidelines, patchy density or milky residue left by uneven development, tired chemistry or careless drying. They follow the flow of liquid rather than the image. Random specks and hairlines are [dust_and_scratches](#dust_and_scratches).

entries.name: expired_film
entries.description: Film used long past its date, so colours drift, contrast drops and base [fog](#fog) lifts the shadows. The effect is uneven and unpredictable across a roll. Deliberate reversed loading is [redscale](#redscale); an even veil from stray light is [fogged_film](#fogged_film).

entries.name: fogged_film
entries.description: The whole frame is veiled by a milky grey or colour cast because the film met light, heat or age before development. Contrast collapses everywhere at once. A localised burn from a single light path is [light_leak](#light_leak).

entries.name: frame_overlap
entries.description: The film did not advance a full frame, so two exposures bleed into each other across a straight vertical join. Often paired with torn sprocket edges. A deliberate stacking of two exposures on one frame is not this.

entries.name: high_speed_film
entries.description: A very sensitive stock chosen for dim light, paying for it with coarse [film_grain](#film_grain) and lower contrast. Typical of indoor, concert and night work on film. If the speed was gained in development instead, tag [push_processing](#push_processing).

entries.name: large_format_film
entries.description: Shot on individual sheets of film in a view camera, one exposure at a time. Expect enormous detail, a wide rebate edge and sometimes film-holder marks along the frame. Rollfilm negatives belong under [medium_format_film](#medium_format_film).

entries.name: negative_image
entries.description: The picture is shown as the negative itself, tones reversed and, on colour stock, sitting under an orange base. Either presented that way deliberately or left unconverted. Once inverted to normal tones, use [film_scan](#film_scan).

entries.name: pinhole_photograph
entries.description: Made through a tiny hole instead of a lens, so the whole frame is uniformly soft, dark towards the corners, and exposed long enough for moving things to smear away. Softness caused by a lens or filter is not this.

entries.name: print_toning
entries.description: The finished print's silver was chemically converted, shifting it warm brown, cool purple, or split between the two. The colour sits in the image, never on the paper base. A [sepia](#sepia) colour grade applied in software is not this.

entries.name: push_processing
entries.description: The film was rated faster than its speed and developed longer to compensate, raising contrast and coarsening [film_grain](#film_grain) while shadows stay empty. Common in low light and reportage. Shorter development for softer results is [pull_processing](#pull_processing).

entries.name: sprocket_holes
entries.description: The perforations along the film edge appear in the picture, from a wide scan or a camera that exposes the full strip width. A clear marker of 35mm material. If only the plain rebate shows, use [film_border](#film_border) instead.

entries.name: cyanotype
entries.description: A hand-coated print in iron chemistry, washed in water to a deep Prussian blue with white highlights, usually exposed in sunlight. Brush marks around the edges are common. Blue reached by treating a silver print is [print_toning](#print_toning).

entries.name: daguerreotype
entries.description: A mirror-polished silver plate whose image flips between positive and negative as it is tilted, normally cased behind glass with tarnish creeping in from the edges. Detail is astonishing. Later metal-plate positives are [tintype](#tintype).

entries.name: edge_markings
entries.description: Frame numbers, stock codes and arrows printed along the film edge are legible in the picture. Useful evidence of the format and the order of frames. Tag [film_border](#film_border) as well when the whole rebate is shown.

entries.name: film_soup
entries.description: The roll was deliberately soaked in liquid, heat or chemicals before development, melting colour into blotches and streaks that run along the strip. Damage is heavy and random. Milder drift from age belongs under [expired_film](#expired_film).

entries.name: half_frame
entries.description: Two narrow upright exposures sit side by side inside one normal 35mm frame and are often [scanned](#scanned) as a pair. Grain is coarse for the picture size. Do not confuse it with [frame_overlap](#frame_overlap), where the advance failed and images bleed together.

entries.name: infrared_film
entries.description: Film sensitive beyond visible red, so foliage records as glowing white and skies go nearly black. Usually shot behind a deep red filter and showing heavy [halation](#halation). Digital infrared conversions do not belong here.

entries.name: lith_print
entries.description: Printed in dilute lith developer and snatched partway, giving gritty hard blacks, delicate warm highlights and heavy visible grain. The colour comes from the development itself. Colour added to a finished print is [print_toning](#print_toning).

entries.name: peel_apart_film
entries.description: Instant material developed between a print and a paper negative that is pulled off and discarded, leaving ragged edges and chemical smears. Distinct from the sealed white-bordered card of [instant_film](#instant_film). The discarded negative is sometimes salvaged and [scanned](#scanned).

entries.name: photogram
entries.description: Objects were laid straight on light-sensitive paper and exposed, leaving pale silhouettes on a dark ground with no camera involved. Edges soften wherever an object stood off the paper. A print made from a negative this way is [contact_print](#contact_print).

entries.name: platinum_print
entries.description: A hand-coated contact print in platinum or palladium salts, with long delicate midtones, a matte surface and the image lying in the paper fibres. Blacks are softer than in a silver [darkroom_print](#darkroom_print). Brushed borders are usual.

entries.name: pull_processing
entries.description: The film was rated slower than its speed and given shorter development, lowering contrast and holding highlight detail. Results look flat and finely grained. The opposite treatment is [push_processing](#push_processing).

entries.name: redscale
entries.description: Colour negative film loaded backwards so light passes through the base first, giving heavy red and orange casts with thin shadows. The shift is even across every frame. Unpredictable colour drift from age is [expired_film](#expired_film).

entries.name: reticulation
entries.description: The emulsion cracked into a fine crazed web after a sudden temperature change in processing, looking like a texture pressed evenly into the whole image. It survives any amount of enlargement. Coarse texture from the stock itself is [film_grain](#film_grain).

entries.name: solarization
entries.description: Part of the image reverses into negative with bright outlines along the boundaries, because the developing material was re-exposed to light partway through. The effect is uneven and follows edges. A software filter imitating it does not belong here.

entries.name: test_strip
entries.description: A strip of printing paper exposed in bands so the same slice of the picture repeats at increasing densities. Made to judge an exposure time, not to keep. A whole roll proofed at once is a [contact_sheet](#contact_sheet).

entries.name: tintype
entries.description: A one-off positive on a blackened metal plate, slightly dull, often scratched or with clipped corners, and laterally reversed. Usually a [portrait](#portrait). On glass rather than metal it is the ambrotype form of [wet_plate_collodion](#wet_plate_collodion).

entries.name: wet_plate_collodion
entries.description: The plate was coated, exposed and developed while still wet, leaving pour lines, thin edges and streaks around the picture. Skies blank out and skin renders pale. A positive of this kind on blackened metal is a [tintype](#tintype).

entries.name: cropped
entries.description: The frame was trimmed after capture, changing the composition or the aspect ratio from what the camera recorded. Use it when the crop is known or obvious, such as a square or extreme panoramic ratio. Levelling the horizon as well is [straightened](#straightened).

entries.name: noise_reduction
entries.description: Grain and speckle were smoothed away in processing, often leaving waxy skin, smeared foliage and a plasticky look in the shadows. Use it when the smoothing is visible or known. The untreated speckle is [digital_noise](#digital_noise).

entries.name: raw_file
entries.description: The picture comes from an unprocessed sensor file rather than a camera-made JPEG, so white balance, tone and sharpening were all decided afterwards. Use it for the source, not for how much editing was done. The camera's own finished file is [in_camera_jpeg](#in_camera_jpeg).

entries.name: retouched
entries.description: Blemishes, stray hairs, dust or small distractions were cleaned away while the frame itself stayed as shot. Ordinary commercial and [portrait](#portrait) finishing. When the retouch reshapes a face or body rather than tidying it, add [body_reshaping](#body_reshaping) or [skin_smoothing](#skin_smoothing).

entries.name: sharpened
entries.description: Edge contrast was raised in processing so detail reads crisper than the lens delivered. Routine on almost every file, so tag it when it is a noticeable part of the look. Overdone sharpening with visible outlines is [oversharpened](#oversharpened).

entries.name: background_removal
entries.description: The subject was cut away from whatever was behind it, leaving flat white, a new backdrop or nothing at all. Very common in product and listing pictures. If the file itself keeps the empty area empty, add [transparent_background](#transparent_background).

entries.name: cloned_out
entries.description: Something present at capture was painted over with pixels borrowed from elsewhere in the frame — a sign, a passer-by, a power line. Look for repeated texture where the object stood. Fills invented by a model rather than copied are [inpainted](#inpainted).

entries.name: composite_image
entries.description: Elements from more than one exposure or source were combined into a single picture — a figure dropped onto another background, objects added that were never there. Use it whenever the frame was never recorded as one shot. Stitched panoramas and merged brackets have their own tags.

entries.name: compression_artifacts
entries.description: Lossy saving has left blocky squares, mosquito noise around edges and smeared colour, usually from repeated re-saving or heavy sizing down. Judge it at full size. Speckle from the sensor instead is [digital_noise](#digital_noise).

entries.name: computational_bokeh
entries.description: Background blur was calculated from a depth map rather than produced by the lens, so it cuts off abruptly at the subject outline and misses hair and glasses. Look at the edges. Real optical blur is [bokeh](#bokeh).

entries.name: digital_noise
entries.description: Visible sensor speckle, usually from a high ISO or a lifted shadow, showing as coloured or luminance grain across flat areas. Use it for the untreated picture. Film-like grain added on purpose is not this.

entries.name: hdr_merge
entries.description: Several frames at different exposures were merged into one file so shadows and highlights both hold detail. This is the merging step, not the look; for the finished appearance use [high_dynamic_range](#high_dynamic_range) or [tone_mapped](#tone_mapped). Frames blended by hand with masks are [exposure_blending](#exposure_blending).

entries.name: heavily_edited
entries.description: The picture has been worked on far past a routine clean-up, so the result is visibly different from anything a camera recorded. Use it as the blanket answer when the specific operations cannot be named. For a picture assembled from several frames use [composite_image](#composite_image).

entries.name: in_camera_jpeg
entries.description: The camera made the finished file itself, baking in its own sharpening, noise reduction and colour profile. Use it when that is known, as the counterpart to [raw_file](#raw_file). It says nothing about later editing, so it can sit beside [retouched](#retouched).

entries.name: local_adjustment
entries.description: Part of the frame was treated differently from the rest through a mask, brush or gradient — a darkened sky, a lifted face. Use it where the selective work is visible. A whole-frame change needs no tag of its own.

entries.name: oversharpened
entries.description: Sharpening went too far: bright halos trace every edge, fine texture crackles and noise is amplified along with detail. Judge it on the halos rather than on how crisp the picture looks. Genuine optical crispness is [tack_sharp](#tack_sharp).

entries.name: panorama_stitch
entries.description: Overlapping frames were joined into one wide or tall picture, usually with a much longer aspect ratio than the camera makes. Look for a very wide frame and bent horizon lines. Visible joins or doubled objects are [stitching_error](#stitching_error).

entries.name: scanned
entries.description: The picture reached the computer through a scanner rather than a camera — a print, a negative or a slide. Look for flat even lighting, paper texture and a border. Repair work on an old scan is [photo_restoration](#photo_restoration).

entries.name: skin_smoothing
entries.description: Skin has been softened past what any lens does, so pores and fine lines are gone and the face looks waxy or plastic. Includes phone beauty modes. Careful work that keeps texture is better tagged [frequency_separation](#frequency_separation).

entries.name: straight_out_of_camera
entries.description: Nothing was changed after capture: no crop, no tonal work, no clean-up. Use it for pictures posted as shot, whatever the file type. If only the tone was left alone but the frame was trimmed, use [cropped](#cropped) instead.

entries.name: straightened
entries.description: The picture was rotated so the horizon or the verticals sit true, which always trims the corners a little. Use it for the correction, not for a frame that was level to begin with. Deliberate tilt is [dutch_angle](#dutch_angle).

entries.name: upscaled
entries.description: The file was enlarged beyond the pixels actually captured, so detail is interpolated rather than recorded. Look for soft mush or over-clean edges at full size. Enlargement done by a trained model is [ai_upscaled](#ai_upscaled).

entries.name: watermarked
entries.description: A name, logo or repeating [pattern](#pattern) was laid over the picture to mark ownership or a preview copy. Use it whatever the mark's size or opacity. A caption or credit line printed in a border is not this.

entries.name: ai_upscaled
entries.description: A model invented the extra pixels, so edges are unnaturally clean, texture is regular and small text or faces come out plausible but wrong. Distinct from plain interpolation, which just goes soft. Compare [upscaled](#upscaled).

entries.name: body_reshaping
entries.description: A face or figure was pushed and pulled out of its recorded shape — a narrowed waist, a slimmed jaw, enlarged eyes. Look for bent lines in the background behind the edited edge. Cleaning blemishes without moving anything is [retouched](#retouched).

entries.name: downscaled
entries.description: The file was reduced from a much larger original, typically for the web, so fine detail is gone and any remaining artifacts are baked in. Use it when the small size is a processing choice rather than the camera's output. See [low_resolution](#low_resolution) sources separately.

entries.name: dust_spot_removal
entries.description: Dark specks from sensor dust or scan debris were healed out, most visible against plain sky. Look for faint soft patches in an otherwise even area. Removing a real object rather than a speck is [cloned_out](#cloned_out).

entries.name: flipped
entries.description: The picture was mirrored left to right, so text reads backwards and any [asymmetry](#asymmetry) is reversed. Selfie cameras do it by default. Check lettering and shirt buttons before applying it.

entries.name: frequency_separation
entries.description: Skin or a surface was split into fine texture and broad tone so blotches could be evened out while the pores stayed. Suspect it where skin looks smooth in the large but still grainy up close. Loss of texture altogether is [skin_smoothing](#skin_smoothing).

entries.name: image_stacking
entries.description: Many frames of the same scene were averaged or combined to cut noise or build up a long effect, common in night and astronomical work. Use it for the multi-frame method itself. Merging different exposures is [hdr_merge](#hdr_merge); merging focus distances is [focus_stacking](#focus_stacking).

entries.name: inpainted
entries.description: A gap in the picture was filled with content generated to match its surroundings rather than copied from another part of the frame. Often used to erase objects or extend an edge. Smeared or nonsensical detail in the filled area gives it away.

entries.name: metadata_stripped
entries.description: The file carries no capture data — no camera, no date, no location — usually because it went through a screenshot, a chat app or a deliberate scrub. Useful to know before trusting any dating or ordering by capture time.

entries.name: moire
entries.description: A fine repeating [pattern](#pattern) — fabric weave, a screen, a distant fence — beats against the pixel grid and produces wavy bands or false colour. Look at shirts and roof tiles. It is a capture and resizing fault, not a deliberate effect.

entries.name: perspective_correction
entries.description: Leaning walls were pulled upright in software, stretching the top of the frame and cutting the corners. Common in architecture and copy work. Lens curvature [straightened](#straightened) instead is [distortion_corrected](#distortion_corrected); verticals left leaning are [converging_verticals](#converging_verticals).

entries.name: photo_restoration
entries.description: A damaged old picture was repaired after scanning: tears mended, creases filled, stains and fading pulled back. Use it for the repaired result. Adding colour to a monochrome original belongs with the colour tags.

entries.name: privacy_blur
entries.description: Faces, plates, screens or documents were blurred, pixelated or blacked out to hide identifying detail. Use it for the deliberate obscuring, wherever it sits in the frame. Blur from the lens or from movement is not this.

entries.name: red_eye_removal
entries.description: The red pupils caused by direct [flash](#flash) were corrected afterwards, sometimes leaving grey or oddly flat eyes. Use it when the fix is visible or known. The uncorrected effect itself is [red_eye](#red_eye).

entries.name: sky_replacement
entries.description: The original sky was cut out and another put in its place, usually a more dramatic one. Tell-tales are edge halos around branches and light on the land that does not match the new sky. A sky merely darkened by a mask is [local_adjustment](#local_adjustment).

entries.name: transparent_background
entries.description: The file carries an alpha channel and the area around the subject is genuinely empty, usually shown as a checkerboard. Use it for the file, not for a subject standing on plain white. A white-filled cutout is [background_removal](#background_removal) alone.

entries.name: deblurred
entries.description: Software tried to undo camera shake or missed focus, recovering edges that the file did not really hold. Look for ringing beside high-contrast edges and an odd etched texture. A picture that is simply soft is not this.

entries.name: stitching_error
entries.description: The join between merged frames failed: a doubled limb, a broken railing, a smeared branch or a step in the horizon. Use it for the visible fault, not for a clean stitch. Common where something moved between frames.

entries.name: high_iso_noise
entries.description: Gritty speckle over the whole picture from a high sensitivity or a heavily lifted exposure, coarsest in the shadows, with fine detail turning mushy. Use it where the noise was not wanted; film-like texture chosen for the look is a different matter.

entries.name: jpeg_artefacts
entries.description: Blocky squares, mosquito fuzz around hard edges and smeared colour, from heavy compression or repeated re-saving. Worst on flat gradients and small text. Stair-stepped diagonals without the blocking are [aliasing](#aliasing).

entries.name: blinked
entries.description: The subject's eyes are closed or half shut at the moment of exposure, or caught mid-blink so the eyes read as slits. One frame of a burst is usually fine. A deliberate closed-eye pose is not this.

entries.name: low_resolution
entries.description: The file simply does not hold enough pixels for what it shows: faces are a few dozen pixels across, text is unreadable, and nothing is recoverable. A thumbnail or a heavily shrunk copy. Enlarging it only adds [pixelation](#pixelation).

entries.name: overprocessed
entries.description: The edit is doing too much and it shows: crunched local contrast, glowing edges, unnatural colour, plastic texture. Use it as the general verdict and add [halo_artefact](#halo_artefact), [heavy_noise_reduction](#heavy_noise_reduction) or [retouching_artefact](#retouching_artefact) for the specific tell.

entries.name: pixelation
entries.description: Individual pixels are visible as squares because the picture was enlarged well past its real size. Edges become staircases of solid blocks. Blocks in groups of eight around detail, with fuzz, are [jpeg_artefacts](#jpeg_artefacts) instead.

entries.name: posterization
entries.description: A smooth gradient breaks into visible steps of flat colour, typically in sky or a studio backdrop, because too few tonal levels survived the edit or the export. Stripes running the full width of the frame from the sensor are [banding_noise](#banding_noise).

entries.name: sensor_dust
entries.description: Soft dark blobs in the same place on every frame, worst in plain sky and at small apertures. They sit on the sensor or its filter rather than on the front glass, so they do not move with the scene. Dirt on the front element is [lens_smudge](#lens_smudge).

entries.name: accidental_shot
entries.description: The shutter fired with nobody framing anything: a pocket, the floor, the ceiling, a smear of ground going past. Usually dark, blurred and formless. Keep it for frames with no intent behind them at all.

entries.name: aliasing
entries.description: Hard edges break into visible stair steps and thin lines flicker in and out of existence, from too little resolution for the detail or a careless downscale. Coloured interference over a repeating [pattern](#pattern) is [moire](#moire) rather than this.

entries.name: animal_eyeshine
entries.description: An animal's eyes glow flat green, yellow or white because the [flash](#flash) bounced off the reflective layer behind the retina. It ruins pet and wildlife frames. The human equivalent is [red_eye](#red_eye).

entries.name: banding_noise
entries.description: Faint horizontal or vertical stripes across shadow areas, coming from the sensor readout rather than from anything in the scene. Usually appears after a big shadow lift. Smooth stepped gradients in a sky are [posterization](#posterization).

entries.name: chroma_noise
entries.description: Blotches of wrong colour, usually red and green, sitting on top of the grain in dark areas. It survives conversion to grey as uneven patchiness. Add [high_iso_noise](#high_iso_noise) when the plain speckle is obvious too.

entries.name: chroma_smear
entries.description: Colour bleeds past the edges it belongs to, so red lettering or a lipstick line looks blurred while the grey detail stays sharp. Comes from the reduced colour resolution of video and low-quality encodes. Add [jpeg_artefacts](#jpeg_artefacts) when blocking shows as well.

entries.name: creased_print
entries.description: A [scanned](#scanned) print carries folds, cracks, torn corners or a bent edge, showing as hard bright lines and missing emulsion. This is damage to the physical object; colour gone off with age is [faded_print](#faded_print).

entries.name: cut_off_subject
entries.description: The frame accidentally clips what matters: half a head, a hand chopped at the wrist, a building sliced through the middle. Read it as a mistake, not as a chosen tight crop of a face or a detail.

entries.name: finger_in_frame
entries.description: A finger or thumb over part of the lens, appearing as a soft pink or dark blob at a corner. Common with phones and compact cameras. For a strap or hood intruding at the edge use [camera_strap_in_frame](#camera_strap_in_frame).

entries.name: flash_blowout
entries.description: The [flash](#flash) was far too strong for the distance, so the nearest surface burns to featureless white while the background falls away black. Faces go chalky and flat. Use it when the flash is the cause rather than the exposure setting.

entries.name: flash_reflection
entries.description: The [flash](#flash) bounces straight back off glass, a spectacle lens, a laminated sign or a whiteboard, leaving a hard white blob over the subject. Shooting square to the surface guarantees it. A wanted highlight in the eye is a [catchlight](#catchlight).

entries.name: halo_artefact
entries.description: A bright or dark outline hugging high-contrast edges, most obvious where a roofline meets sky. Left behind by aggressive sharpening or local contrast work. If the whole frame looks crunchy as well, add [overprocessed](#overprocessed).

entries.name: hdr_ghosting
entries.description: Transparent doubles of anything that moved between the frames of a bracket or a stack: leaves, water, walking people. The merge could not reconcile them. Reflections thrown inside the lens by a bright source are a separate thing.

entries.name: heavy_noise_reduction
entries.description: Noise smoothed away along with the detail: waxy skin, smeared foliage, watercolour blotches where texture should be. Common in phone output and rescued dark frames. The grain it was fighting is [high_iso_noise](#high_iso_noise).

entries.name: lens_fogging
entries.description: The whole frame goes milky and flat because condensation formed on cold glass, typically on carrying the camera into a warm room. It clears from the edges as the lens warms. Fog and [mist](#mist) in the scene itself are weather, not this.

entries.name: lens_smudge
entries.description: A fingerprint or greasy wipe mark on the front glass, softening one region and smearing bright lights across it. Often only obvious against a light source. Spots that hold the same position on every frame are [sensor_dust](#sensor_dust).

entries.name: photobomb
entries.description: Someone walked into the picture, leaned in or was passing behind the subject at the wrong moment. Also covers a stray head or arm at the edge that was not meant to be there. Deliberate group horseplay is not this.

entries.name: retouching_artefact
entries.description: The repair is visible: cloned patches that repeat, warped background lines beside a reshaped body, a smeared area where something was painted out. Straight edges bending near the fix give it away. Add [overprocessed](#overprocessed) if the whole edit is heavy.

entries.name: upscaling_artefact
entries.description: Detail that is waxy, over-clean or plainly invented because the picture was enlarged past what it held; edges look drawn on and textures repeat. Honest enlargement with visible squares is [pixelation](#pixelation).

entries.name: amp_glow
entries.description: A warm magenta or greenish [haze](#haze) creeping in from one corner of a long dark exposure, from sensor electronics warming up. Night and astro frames show it most. Even speckle spread over the whole frame is [high_iso_noise](#high_iso_noise).

entries.name: black_frame
entries.description: The frame came out effectively empty: all black, all white, or a featureless blur, because the [flash](#flash) failed, the cap was on or the camera was moving. Nothing in it is recoverable. A dark but readable picture is simply [underexposed](#underexposed).

entries.name: black_sun
entries.description: The disc of the sun or another blinding source renders dark grey or black with a bright ring around it, because the photosites saturated and the readout wrapped. Usually a phone or an older sensor pointed straight at the sun.

entries.name: flash_orbs
entries.description: Pale translucent discs floating over the frame where the [flash](#flash) lit dust, [rain](#rain) or snow close to the lens, strongest when the flash sits near the lens axis. They land in different places every frame, unlike [sensor_dust](#sensor_dust).

entries.name: frame_tearing
entries.description: A horizontal seam splits the picture, with everything below it shifted sideways, because the capture caught two refreshes of a screen at once. Seen in screen grabs and phone photographs of monitors. The offset is clean and straight.

entries.name: hot_pixel
entries.description: Single bright or coloured points that never move between frames, from a misbehaving photosite. Most visible in long exposures and in dark areas. Scattered coloured speckle that changes from frame to frame is [chroma_noise](#chroma_noise) instead.

entries.name: interlacing_artefact
entries.description: Horizontal comb teeth along anything that moved, because two interlaced fields captured a moment apart were shown as one frame. Almost always a still taken from older video. The edges are sharp and toothed, not blurred.

entries.name: newton_rings
entries.description: Concentric [rainbow](#rainbow) rings where film pressed against glass in a scanner or a slide mount and a thin air gap set up interference. Small, oily-looking and local to the contact patch, unlike the broad shimmer of [moire](#moire).

entries.name: sensor_reflection
entries.description: A regular grid of small red or white dots beside a strong point light, bounced between the sensor surface and the rear of the filter stack. The [pattern](#pattern) is evenly spaced, which is what separates it from ordinary flare blobs.

entries.name: fog
entries.description: Thick airborne water that swallows the background within a short distance, so shapes emerge as flat grey outlines with almost no contrast. Use [mist](#mist) for the thinner version that still lets you read the far distance, and [haze](#haze) for dry particles rather than water.

entries.name: rain
entries.description: Falling rain in the frame or unmistakably on the scene, whether streaked, frozen into droplets, or read through soaked surfaces and raised umbrellas. Use [downpour](#downpour) for a heavy burst and [drizzle](#drizzle) for the fine kind that barely shows.

entries.name: wet_ground
entries.description: Rain-soaked pavement, road or stone acting as a mirror for lights, signs and figures, with colours deepened by the water film. Tag [puddles](#puddles) instead when discrete pools of standing water carry the [reflection](#reflection).

entries.name: aerial_perspective
entries.description: Successive ridges, buildings or trees separating into paler, lower-contrast layers as they recede, the depth cue that [haze](#haze) gives you for free. Tag it when those stacked layers are the point of the picture rather than just present in it.

entries.name: frost
entries.description: White [ice](#ice) crystals grown on grass, leaves, railings or paint overnight, picking out every edge and vein. Different from [snow_cover](#snow_cover), which is fallen and lies in depth, and from [dew](#dew), which is liquid.

entries.name: haze
entries.description: Dry suspended particles that wash out distant contrast and drain colour toward pale blue or yellow. Distinct from [fog](#fog) and [mist](#mist), which are water; if the picture is specifically about the receding tonal layers, tag [aerial_perspective](#aerial_perspective) as well.

entries.name: mist
entries.description: A thin veil of water in the air that softens the distance without hiding it, often lying low over ground or water in the early hours. Reach for [fog](#fog) when the far background is gone entirely.

entries.name: puddles
entries.description: Standing pools of water after [rain](#rain), usually used as a reflecting surface or shot low so the pool fills the foreground. Use [wet_ground](#wet_ground) for a generally soaked surface with no separate pool to point at.

entries.name: rain_on_glass
entries.description: Drops and runnels on a window, windscreen or bus shelter, with the world behind them broken into blur and tiny inverted lenses. The glass is between camera and subject; [water_on_lens](#water_on_lens) is when the drops are on the front element instead.

entries.name: snow_cover
entries.description: Settled snow blanketing ground, roofs or branches, simplifying the scene to shapes and pushing the exposure high. Say [snowfall](#snowfall) instead when flakes are in the air; the two often apply together.

entries.name: snowfall
entries.description: Snow actually falling, read as flakes suspended in the air or streaking past a dark background, often flattening contrast across the whole frame. Use [snow_cover](#snow_cover) for settled snow with nothing coming down.

entries.name: storm_clouds
entries.description: Heavy dark cloud, an anvil head or an advancing squall line dominating the sky, with weather clearly on its way. This is the cloud as subject; the dramatic under-lit light such a sky produces belongs to the natural light tags.

entries.name: windy
entries.description: Wind visible in the scene through blown hair, bent grass, straining flags and driven spray, even when the picture is otherwise sharp. Use the motion tags for the streaking itself; this one records the condition on the day.

entries.name: dew
entries.description: Condensation beaded on grass, webs, leaves or metal after a cold night, often catching low light as a field of tiny highlights. Not [rain](#rain): nothing fell, and the ground beneath is usually dry.

entries.name: downpour
entries.description: Heavy [rain](#rain) hitting hard enough to bounce off the ground, blur the background and drive people under cover. Reserve it for the visibly violent kind; ordinary falling rain is just rain.

entries.name: drizzle
entries.description: Fine, slow [rain](#rain) that rarely registers as streaks and shows up instead as damp surfaces, a flat grey sky and beaded clothing. Choose rain or [downpour](#downpour) when the drops themselves are visible.

entries.name: heat_haze
entries.description: Rippling, wobbling distortion above hot ground, tarmac or an engine, which makes distant subjects shimmer and refuse to resolve no matter how good the focus is. Not the same as [haze](#haze), which dulls contrast but keeps edges straight.

entries.name: ice
entries.description: Frozen water as a surface or mass in the scene: sheeted [puddles](#puddles), an iced-over lake, icicles or a glazed road. Use [frost](#frost) for the crystalline coating on things and [snow_cover](#snow_cover) for settled flakes.

entries.name: rainbow
entries.description: A rainbow arc across the scene, needing sun behind the camera and [rain](#rain) or spray in front of it, sometimes doubled or shortened to a bright fragment. Tag it whenever the bow is legible, even if it is only a stub over a hillside.

entries.name: smog
entries.description: Urban air pollution sitting over a city as a brown or grey band, flattening the [skyline](#skyline) and tinting everything beyond a few blocks. Use plain [haze](#haze) for clean atmospheric distance and [smoke_haze](#smoke_haze) when the source is fire.

entries.name: smoke_haze
entries.description: Wildfire or field smoke filling the air, usually pushing the whole frame orange or [sepia](#sepia) and reddening the sun. Different from [smog](#smog), which is traffic and industry, and from [fog](#fog), which is water and stays neutral grey.

entries.name: steam
entries.description: Vapour rising visibly from vents, drains, water, animals or a warm surface into cold air, often catching light as a bright plume. Distinguish it from [mist](#mist), which is settled in the air, and from [smoke_haze](#smoke_haze), which is combustion.

entries.name: visible_breath
entries.description: Exhaled vapour showing as a small cloud in cold air, best read when [backlit](#backlit) against a dark background. A cheap and reliable way of saying how cold the day was, and worth tagging separately from [frost](#frost) or [snow_cover](#snow_cover).

entries.name: water_on_lens
entries.description: Drops or spray sitting on the front of the lens or filter, showing as soft blurred blobs and smeared flare that no focus setting can fix. Distinct from [rain_on_glass](#rain_on_glass), where the water is on a pane the camera is shooting through.

entries.name: blizzard
entries.description: Wind-driven snow dense enough to erase the background and reduce the picture to near-white with a few dark shapes in it. Reserve it for whiteout conditions; ordinary flakes coming down are [snowfall](#snowfall).

entries.name: cloud_inversion
entries.description: Cloud or [fog](#fog) pooled in a valley below the camera with peaks and ridges standing out of it, shot from a summit or an aircraft. It is fog seen from above, so tag it rather than fog when the viewpoint is the whole point.

entries.name: dust_storm
entries.description: Wind-lifted sand or dust thick enough to obscure the scene, arriving as a visible wall or a general ochre blanket. Use it for the event; [haze](#haze) covers ordinary dry particulate sitting in still air.

entries.name: flooded_ground
entries.description: Water standing over ground that should be dry, covering a street, field or path after prolonged [rain](#rain). Larger and more consequential than [puddles](#puddles), and it usually turns the whole foreground into a reflecting surface.

entries.name: frost_on_glass
entries.description: Feathered [ice](#ice) patterns on a window or windscreen, usually shot [backlit](#backlit) so the crystal structure reads against a bright outside. A close cousin of [frost](#frost), singled out because the glass turns it into a graphic subject in itself.

entries.name: hail
entries.description: Ice pellets falling or lying scattered on ground, car roofs and leaves after a storm has passed. Larger and harder-edged than [sleet](#sleet), and unlike [snow_cover](#snow_cover) it sits as separate stones rather than a blanket.

entries.name: lightning
entries.description: A visible discharge in the frame, branching to ground or spreading inside cloud, usually caught on a long open shutter. Use [storm_clouds](#storm_clouds) for a threatening sky with no strike recorded.

entries.name: sea_spray
entries.description: Airborne salt water off breaking waves, hanging as a bright [haze](#haze) over the shoreline and softening everything behind it. Shot from close in it usually comes with [water_on_lens](#water_on_lens) as well.

entries.name: sleet
entries.description: Half-melted snow or icy [rain](#rain), which soaks surfaces the way rain does while still showing white in the air. Use it for the messy in-between; clean flakes are [snowfall](#snowfall) and clear drops are rain.

entries.name: behind_the_scenes
entries.description: A picture of the shoot rather than the shot: gear, crew or the subject being posed, all visible at once. Use it for the making-of frame; if only one piece of kit strayed into an otherwise finished picture, tag that item instead.

entries.name: camera_in_mirror
entries.description: The camera or phone taking the picture appears in a mirror, window or other reflective surface. The classic self-portrait shape, with the device usually covering part of the face. If the shooter shows but not the camera, use [photographer_in_frame](#photographer_in_frame).

entries.name: camera_visible
entries.description: A camera, lens or phone held up to shoot appears somewhere in the frame — around a subject's neck, on a table, or in someone else's hands. Use [camera_in_mirror](#camera_in_mirror) for the reflected self-portrait case.

entries.name: light_stand_visible
entries.description: A lighting stand, its legs or a grip arm show in the picture. Tag the stand even when the head on top is [cropped](#cropped) away; if the modifier itself is visible use [softbox_in_shot](#softbox_in_shot), [umbrella_in_shot](#umbrella_in_shot) or [reflector_in_shot](#reflector_in_shot) as well.

entries.name: photographer_in_frame
entries.description: The person making the picture is visible in it — reflected, casting into a corner, or standing in a wide making-of view. Use [photographer's_shadow](#photographer's_shadow) when only the [silhouette](#silhouette) on the ground gives them away.

entries.name: reflector_in_shot
entries.description: A collapsible disc or panel bouncing light is visible, sometimes held by an assistant at the edge of the frame. Silver, white or gold faces all count. If it is a translucent panel between lamp and subject, use [diffusion_panel_in_shot](#diffusion_panel_in_shot).

entries.name: seamless_paper
entries.description: A roll of studio paper is visible as a physical object — the tube overhead, the curved sweep onto the floor, or a torn and scuffed edge underfoot. Use it when the paper reads as equipment rather than as a clean background.

entries.name: softbox_in_shot
entries.description: A boxed or octagonal diffuser is visible in the frame, not merely inferred from the quality of the light. Tag the light's effect separately; this one is only about the object being in the picture.

entries.name: tripod_visible
entries.description: A tripod or its legs appear in the frame, whether another photographer's or the shooter's own caught in a [reflection](#reflection). Use [camera_in_mirror](#camera_in_mirror) when the reflection is the point of the picture.

entries.name: backdrop_edge_visible
entries.description: The backdrop runs out inside the frame: its edge, corner, crease or the wall and floor beyond it are all in the picture. Tag it when the illusion of an endless background breaks; [backdrop_stand_visible](#backdrop_stand_visible) covers the supporting hardware.

entries.name: backdrop_stand_visible
entries.description: The crossbar, uprights or clamps holding a backdrop appear in the picture. Often paired with [backdrop_edge_visible](#backdrop_edge_visible) in a wide frame that shows the whole rig rather than a [cropped](#cropped) background.

entries.name: cable_in_shot
entries.description: Power leads, sync cords or extension runs snake across the floor or dangle from a stand inside the frame. A common giveaway that a picture was not [retouched](#retouched) or the set not cleaned up.

entries.name: camera_strap_in_frame
entries.description: A strap has swung in front of the lens and hangs across a corner of the picture, usually dark and out of focus. An accident rather than a subject; if the whole camera is in the picture use [camera_visible](#camera_visible).

entries.name: film_crew_visible
entries.description: Assistants, stylists or a whole crew are at work inside the frame, adjusting lights, holding gear or touching up the subject. Tag it for the working bodies; the gear itself gets its own tags alongside.

entries.name: flash_head_in_shot
entries.description: A bare [strobe](#strobe) head, monolight or clip-on [flash](#flash) unit is visible in the frame. Includes a hot-shoe unit seen on another photographer's camera. For the modifier mounted on it use [softbox_in_shot](#softbox_in_shot) or [umbrella_in_shot](#umbrella_in_shot) instead.

entries.name: photographer's_shadow
entries.description: The shadow of the person shooting, and often of the camera or tripod, falls into the bottom of the frame. Typical of low sun at the photographer's back. Distinct from [photographer_in_frame](#photographer_in_frame), where the body itself is seen.

entries.name: ring_light_in_shot
entries.description: The ring lamp itself is in the picture, typically behind or around a phone or camera in a self-portrait setup. Tag this only for the visible fixture; the ring-shaped [catchlight](#catchlight) it leaves in the eyes is a lighting matter.

entries.name: studio_setup_shot
entries.description: The lighting arrangement itself is the subject — stands, modifiers and backdrop photographed as a record of how a picture was lit. Often shot from behind the camera position. Narrower than [behind_the_scenes](#behind_the_scenes), which also covers crew and subject at work.

entries.name: umbrella_in_shot
entries.description: A shoot-through or bounce umbrella appears in the picture, its ribbed shape unmistakable behind or beside the subject. Only for the umbrella being seen; the softer light it produces belongs to a lighting tag.

entries.name: beauty_dish_in_shot
entries.description: The shallow metal dish with its centre deflector is visible in the frame. Recognisable by the round rim and the small plate suspended in front of the bulb. Use only when the dish is seen, not when its light is merely characteristic.

entries.name: boom_arm_visible
entries.description: An arm reaching over the subject to hang a light or modifier overhead is in frame. Usually counterweighted and slanting in from one edge. Distinct from [light_stand_visible](#light_stand_visible), where the upright column is what shows.

entries.name: clapperboard
entries.description: A slate held up in front of the lens, chalked or printed with take information. Marks a frame as a production record rather than a finished picture.

entries.name: color_checker_in_frame
entries.description: A calibration chart or grey card is held in the scene so the shot can be balanced later. Usually a first frame of a run, with the subject waiting behind it. Not a finished picture, and worth excluding from most selections.

entries.name: diffusion_panel_in_shot
entries.description: A translucent scrim or silk stretched on a frame stands between a lamp and the subject and is visible in the picture. Distinguish from [reflector_in_shot](#reflector_in_shot), which bounces light back rather than passing it through.
